detail.abstract:
Corporate legal departments face a structural dilemma: their most valuable contributions are preventive and counterfactual, yet existing reporting systems are not designed to capture absence as value. While external legal services appear as measurable expenses, internal legal functions are evaluated under the same cost-based logic, creating a persistent gap between legal impact and its observable representation.

Existing maturity frameworks, such as those developed by ACC and CLOC, have focused primarily on internal legal operations, offering structured approaches to process optimization, technology adoption, and cost control. However, they provide limited explanatory power in contexts characterized by high regulatory complexity, constrained resources, and asymmetric workload distribution, particularly in emerging market environments.

This paper introduces the Corporate Legal Service Maturity Model (CLS-MM), a design science framework that reconceptualizes legal maturity as a property of legal service delivery across the organization, rather than of legal operations alone. The model proposes four maturity stages and eight diagnostic dimensions, complemented by ten diagnostic metrics, including three novel indicators designed to capture resource–complexity asymmetries. By shifting the analytical focus toward the legal–business interface, the CLS-MM offers a diagnostic and prescriptive tool for assessing legal effectiveness in complex organizational settings.

title: When Better AI Hurts: Verification, Compliance, and AI-Human Handoffs in Service Systems
affiliations: University of Rochester - Simon Business School, University of Connecticut - Department of Operations & Information Management, University of Rochester - Simon Business School and University of Connecticut - Department of Operations & Information Management

detail.title: When Better AI Hurts: Verification, Compliance, and AI-Human Handoffs in Service Systems
detail.abstract: Generative AI agents deployed in customer-facing services introduce a distinctive failure mode: hallucination risk, whereby AI responses appear plausible and complete yet may be incorrect, with correctness unobservable prior to human verification. We develop a game-theoretic queueing model of AI-human handoffs in which a firm sets a verification policy and strategic, delay-sensitive customers decide whether to bypass human review and exit with unverified AI answers. Our central finding is an AI improvement trap: when hallucination risk exceeds a critical threshold, improving AI accuracy can paradoxically reduce the effective throughput, which is the rate of successful service completions. The mechanism operates through equilibrium responses: more reliable AI makes customers more willing to forgo human verification, compelling the firm to change its verification policy to maintain compliance. This equilibrium adjustment expands unverified completions, and the resulting errors can outweigh the direct accuracy gains. Consumer surplus, however, always increases with AI accuracy, revealing a firm-customer incentive misalignment: firms may rationally resist AI investments that benefit customers. We further extend the model to incorporate several distinctive features of GenAI systems, including AI reasoning, feedback learning, and imperfect difficulty assessment. These extensions reveal that enhancing AI capability does not automatically improve operational performance. Instead, the benefits of better AI depend critically on how improvements reshape customer behavior and firm policies, reinforcing the central role of strategic responses in determining system outcomes.

title: A Policy Design Framework for Effective Ethical Governance of Artificial Intelligence in Defence
affiliations: , Oxford internet Institute and University of Oxford - Oxford Internet Institute

detail.title: A Policy Design Framework for Effective Ethical Governance of Artificial Intelligence in Defence

declarations.funderStatement: Antonia-Felicia Toffert, Cyril Birks, and Mariarosaria Taddeo have been funded by the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory (Dstl). The research underpinning this work was funded by the UK Defence Chief Scientific Advisor’s Science and Technology Portfolio, through the Dstl Autonomy Programme

detail.abstract: Ethical governance of artificial intelligence (AI) in defence must be legitimate under democratic standards and effective under operational pressure. The values it should serve are largely settled, as reflected in Just War Theory, International Humanitarian Law, and a convergent body of AI ethics. What is missing are the procedures to bind those principles to authoritative decision, institutional responsibility, and operational constraint. The deficit is therefore procedural, not substantive. In this article, we focus on ethical governance as a problem of policy design. Any such design must address three non-substitutable problems, those of knowledge, of authority and accountability, and of justification, each dominant at a different stage of the policy process: knowledge at inception, justification at deliberation, authority and accountability at operationalisation. We argue that defence does not create new problems but intensifies these, through recurring conditions such as operational tempo, secrecy, and coalition fragmentation that raise their difficulty without altering their kind. From this we build a stage-differentiated framework anchored by three instruments, a Non-Delegable Normative Decisions Register that records the substantive limits no procedure may override, diagonal-tiered transparency and accountability structures that allocate authority and extend scrutiny beyond the chain of command, and an Operational Requirements and Constraints Specification that converts those commitments into auditable parameters. The framework secures legitimacy through compliance with its procedures and makes its effectiveness assessable, so failures of either kind become visible and answerable.

title: When the Scaffold Stays On: AI, Practice Style, and Screening in Elite Skill Formation

detail.title: When the Scaffold Stays On: AI, Practice Style, and Screening in Elite Skill Formation
detail.abstract: Generative AI raises short-term productivity by completing tasks that learners would otherwise practice on their own. Whether this substitution erodes frontier skill, the skill required for top-tail non-AI-aided performance, is an open question with growing stakes wherever AI is unavailable or insufficient. The sharper question, however, is whether selection mechanisms can screen apart two coexisting types: substitute-users, who use AI in place of deliberate practice, and complement-users, who use it to accelerate skill development. We exploit a feature of elite programming. The International Collegiate Programming Contest (ICPC) and the International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI) prohibit AI under in-person proctoring and admit entrants through qualification rounds, whereas online Codeforces (CF) contests are unproctored and open to all. From CF submission histories we build an AI-prompt signature, marked by more first-attempt acceptances and fewer attempts and debugging retries, consistent with AI-assisted practice. Three patterns triangulate an institutional-screening mechanism. First, CF practice has shifted toward this signature across entry cohorts spanning two AI rollouts. Second, in open CF contests a stronger signature predicts smaller CF rating gains for users with no ICPC or IOI affiliation, but not for users who qualified for those AI-prohibited contests. Third, inside the AI-prohibited ICPC environment, a shift toward this AI-style practice predicts higher non-AI-aided scores for AI-era entrants. The same practice input thus carries opposite signs depending on whether the contest environment screens for it. The contrast points to two levers: how AI is integrated into training, since within the screened pool AI-style practice coincides with stronger non-AI-aided performance; and the design of AI-prohibited evaluation gates as a type-separating institution. Both extend beyond competitive programming to credentialing systems, from medical and legal boards to professional certification, that must certify skill in a workforce whose practice is increasingly shaped by AI.

title: Quality of Healthy Work Environment and Related Factors in Clinical Nurses: A Structural Equation Modeling
affiliations: Sahmyook University and Sahmyook University

detail.title: Quality of Healthy Work Environment and Related Factors in Clinical Nurses: A Structural Equation Modeling
detail.abstract: Background: This study examined factors associated with the quality of healthy work environments (HWE) among clinical nurses in South Korea using structural equation modeling based on Ferrans’ Health-Related Quality of Life Model. Objective: To identify factors influencing HWE quality and test a structural equation model. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted with 299 nurses from general hospitals in Seoul and Gyeonggi. Data were collected using validated questionnaires measuring nursing need satisfaction, job satisfaction, nursing performance, subjective health status, nursing work environment, and HWE quality. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the validity of the measurement model. Results: Nursing need satisfaction (β = .19, p < .01) and job satisfaction (β = .64, p < .001) were positively associated with the nursing work environment, which was significantly related to HWE quality (β = .26, p < .05). Nursing performance had a direct association with HWE quality (β = .15, p < .01). Job satisfaction showed both direct and indirect effects on HWE quality. The model explained 45% of the variance in the nursing work environment and 51% in HWE quality. Conclusion: Strategies including educational programs, leadership training, and workload optimization may improve HWE quality, nurse retention, and patient care outcomes.

title: Birch Bark Biocomposite Filament for Additive Manufacturing: Properties, Comparative Analysis, Economic Outlook and Applications
affiliations: Russian Academy of National Economy and Public Administration under the President of the Russian Federation (RANEPA)

detail.title: Birch Bark Biocomposite Filament for Additive Manufacturing: Properties, Comparative Analysis, Economic Outlook and Applications
detail.abstract: Birch bark (Betula pendula Roth.) outer bark is an abundant forestry by-product whose primary constituent, the biopolyester suberin, imparts exceptional hydrophobicity, UV resistance and intrinsic antimicrobial activity. Despite growing interest in plant-based biocomposite filaments for fused deposition modelling (FDM), birch bark has not yet been systematically evaluated as a filler for polylactic acid (PLA) filament. This study presents a conceptual and literaturebased characterisation of birch bark/PLA biocomposite filaments (10-20 wt.% filler) and benchmarks their projected properties against established wood-based FDM filaments (sawdust/PLA, bamboo/PLA and cork/PLA). Key physicochemical and mechanical parameters examined include density, tensile strength, Young's modulus, flexural strength, water absorption, moisture resistance and biodegradability. Projected tensile strength of 38-46 MPa and density of 1.15-1.22 g/cm³ position the birch-bark composite as superior to cork/PLA in strength while approaching wood/PLA values, with markedly better moisture resistance than cellulose-rich fillers. An economic analysis reveals that the global biocomposite market, valued at USD 33-44 billion in 2025 (CAGR ~14-18 %), and the 3D printing filament market, expected to reach USD 3.2-26.8 billion by 2031-2035, together constitute a significant commercial opportunity. Raw material costs are additionally favourable because outer bark represents industrial waste currently incinerated in pulp mills. Prospective application domains encompass sustainable packaging, cultural heritage restoration, interior design, biomedical auxiliaries and educational models. The results support further experimental investigation of birch-bark/PLA filament and its integration into both industrial manufacturing and traditional craft revival programmes.

title: Dual Representation of Robust Risk Measures and Uncertainty Sets
affiliations: Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS), Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS) and

detail.title: Dual Representation of Robust Risk Measures and Uncertainty Sets
detail.abstract: We consider robust risk measures that arise as worst-case values of convex risk measures evaluated on uncertainty sets. We characterize continuity properties of robust risk measures through their consolidated uncertainty sets, derive dual representations for robust risk measures, and develop a set-valued dual representation for consolidated uncertainty sets. The two dual frameworks rely on distinct geometric assumptions and are therefore complementary rather than interchangeable.

title: Securing the Future to Risk the Present? Retirement Plans and Entrepreneurial Risk-taking
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Lowell - Department of Finance and

detail.title: Securing the Future to Risk the Present? Retirement Plans and Entrepreneurial Risk-taking
detail.abstract:
This paper examines whether small business owners' adoption of retirement plans (SEP IRA, Solo
401(k)) influences risk-taking behavior in their primary ventures. We hypothesize that securing
personal retirement reduces background financial anxiety, potentially enabling more aggressive
business strategies, a mechanism grounded in the background risk literature. Using the 2019 and
2022 waves of the Survey of Consumer Finances and administrative records from Department of
Labor Form 5500 filings, we measure business risk-taking through three outcomes: financial
leverage, capital investment intensity, and wealth concentration. We exploit the December 2019
SECURE Act as a policy discontinuity, employing a difference-in-differences design that
compares plan-adopting and non-adopting owners before and after the Act's passage.
Our preliminary findings do not detect statistically significant associations between retirement plan
adoption and business risk-taking across any of our three outcome measures, in either cross-
sectional or difference-in-differences specifications. However, the leverage coefficient is
consistently positive across all specifications, directionally consistent with the background risk
hypothesis. Heterogeneity analysis reveals a potentially important age dynamic: owners over 50
who adopt retirement plans exhibit lower leverage relative to younger adopters (coefficient -0.111,
p = 0.134), suggesting that for retirement-vulnerable older owners, plan adoption may operate as
a conservative financial anchor rather than a risk-enabling mechanism. Owners with high prior
wealth concentration in their business show positive but insignificant effects, consistent with the
hypothesized mechanism.
We interpret these null results as informative rather than conclusive. The two-wave design, while
exploiting a clean policy discontinuity, may be insufficient to detect behavioral changes that
operate over longer horizons. These results motivate a richer research design using restricted-
access SCF geographic files, additional survey waves, and Census-linked administrative data. Our
findings contribute to the literature on household finance and entrepreneurship by providing the
first direct empirical test of the retirement security and entrepreneurial risk-taking nexus, and by
identifying heterogeneity by owner age that challenges uniform application of the background risk
mechanism.

title: Job Satisfaction and Organizational Commitment as Determinants of Intention to Leave and Employee Attrition: Evidence from the Steel Industry of Chhattisgarh
affiliations: and AMITY UNIVERSITY CHHATTISGARH

detail.title: Job Satisfaction and Organizational Commitment as Determinants of Intention to Leave and Employee Attrition: Evidence from the Steel Industry of Chhattisgarh
detail.abstract: Employee attrition remains one of the most operationally disruptive and financially costly challenges facing organizations in steel manufacturing. This study empirically examines the determinants of employee attrition in the steel industry of Chhattisgarh, India, focusing on job satisfaction (JS) and organizational commitment (OC) as primary antecedents, mediated through intention to leave (ITL). A structured questionnaire was administered to 120 employees drawn through stratified random sampling across managerial, supervisory, and workmen strata. Primary data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). All five directional hypotheses were supported. JS (beta =-0.214, p < 0.05) and OC (beta =-0.311, p < 0.01) each exerted significant negative effects on ITL. ITL demonstrated an exceptionally strong positive effect on actual attrition (beta = 0.703, p < 0.001). Mediation analyses confirmed that ITL significantly mediates both the JS-attrition and OC-attrition pathways. Strata-wise analysis revealed that workmen exhibit the highest attrition risk (ITL mean = 3.11), while managerial employees are the most satisfied and committed. These findings contribute context-specific empirical evidence to the retention literature and offer actionable recommendations for HR practitioners in the steel sector.

detail.title: Equity Returns with a Trailing Stop-Loss

detail.abstract: This paper studies the effect of a trailing stop-loss on equity returns and risk. Explicit expressions are derived for the expected return, variance and Sharpe ratio under geometric Brownian motion and a regime-switching model. Under constant drift, the results suggest that a trailing stop-loss is generally detrimental despite limiting drawdowns. However, when market conditions can deteriorate or when the sign of the drift is uncertain, a trailing stop-loss can increase expected return while reducing P&L volatility. The paper also shows how to optimise the trailing stop-loss level for either expected return or Sharpe ratio.

title: The Determining Factors of Work Life Balance and the Impacts on Academic Engagement Among Working University Students by PLS-SEM Approach

detail.title: The Determining Factors of Work Life Balance and the Impacts on Academic Engagement Among Working University Students by PLS-SEM Approach
detail.abstract: The increased phenomenon of university students who take professional working jobs outside the university academic responsibilities creates a need to explore and understand the factors which contributing into their success, both in their financial, life balance, and academic engagement. This study aims to examine the impact of Role Clarity, Workplace Culture and Environment, and Stress Management on Work-Life Balance to see the forward effect on the students' academic engagement. The quantitative approach is used to determine the data gained from 70 working university students, by implementing the PLS-SEM Algorithm in SmartPLS 4 software. The purification and bootstrapping methods are also used in the analysis process. The results of this study showed that the Workplace Culture and Environment had the biggest significant positive impact on Work-Life Balance. However, the Stress Management showed no significant effect on statistics. While the Work-Life Balance is significantly affecting the students' Academic Engagement, it is negative due to the indicator phrasing. Moreover, the model showed that the variances were on the value of 46.2% on Work-Life Balance and 51.2% on Academic Engagement. Hence, this study concludes that the Workplace Culture and Environment is more vital to maintain the students' Work Life Balance than the individual strategy of stress management, which suggests the need for workplace flexibility.

title: Food Banks and New Technologies: The Case of FoodFinder
affiliations: University of West Attica

detail.title: Food Banks and New Technologies: The Case of FoodFinder
detail.abstract: Food waste is a major social and environmental problem. At the same time, many people struggle to meet basic nutritional needs. Food Banks contribute to reducing food waste by collecting and distributing food to individuals and families in need. In recent years, new technologies have significantly helped the operation of these organizations through digital platforms and applications. This paper presents the role of Food Banks and examines the FoodFinder application as a case study. The application helps users locate food supply structures in their area, utilizing digital maps and geolocation services. The results show that technology can effectively support social service actions and facilitate citizens' access to food assistance services.

title: Cybersecurity Vulnerabilities in Cloud-Assisted Autonomous Vehicle Routing: Backdoor Attacks on AI Super Networks for Route Manipulation

detail.title: Cybersecurity Vulnerabilities in Cloud-Assisted Autonomous Vehicle Routing: Backdoor Attacks on AI Super Networks for Route Manipulation
detail.abstract: The integration of cloud-assisted artificial intelligence into autonomous vehicle (AV) routing systems promises unprecedented gains in traffic efficiency, energy optimization, and real-time hazard avoidance. However, this architectural shift introduces a critical and underexplored attack surface: the AI super network-a federated or centralized deep learning backbone that fuses global traffic data, vehicular telemetry, and environmental sensors to compute optimal routes. In this work, we expose a novel class of cybersecurity threats wherein adversaries inject backdoor triggers into the training or inference pipeline of these super networks, enabling stealthy, large-scale route manipulation. Unlike conventional GPS spoofing or denial-ofservice attacks, backdoor attacks remain dormant under normal conditions and are activated only by specific spatiotemporal patterns (e.g., subtle weather artifacts, digital map overlays, or synchronized beacon signals), causing targeted AVs to reroute into congested zones, restricted areas, or collision-prone corridors without triggering anomaly detectors. We formalize a threat model for cloud-assisted AV routing, propose three backdoor injection strategies-trainingdata poisoning, model-weight trojaning via federated updates, and adversarial input perturbation during inference-and evaluate their effectiveness on a simulated urban-scale routing environment using real-world traffic datasets. Our results demonstrate that a single backdoor trigger can divert up to 78% of affected AV fleets with less than 0.5% deviation in nominal routing metrics, evading both statistical and learning-based detection baselines. This research underscores that AI super networks, despite their intelligence, are brittle under coordinated backdoor compromise, demanding a paradigm shift in secure V2X (vehicle-toeverything) architecture design.

detail.abstract: This paper implements and extends the Heterogeneous Autoregressive Realized Volatility (HAR-RV) framework for COMEX Gold futures (GC) using live daily data spanning 2021-2026. We augment the HAR benchmark with the CBOE Gold Volatility Index (GVZ), bipower variation jump decomposition, Ridge regression regularization, and geopolitical risk proxies, following Corsi (2009), Luo, Qin and Ye (2016), Wei, Liang et al. (2020), and Gkillas, Gupta and Pierdzioch (2020). Across seven competing specifications, GVZ-augmented models improve out-of-sample R² by 10-56 percentage points relative to the HAR-RV benchmark; Ridge regression achieves the largest improvement (+55.6%) though without conventional statistical significance under the Clark-West (2007) test. The AR-GVZ specification achieves marginal significance (p = 0.065). A key practitioner contribution distinguishes volatility forecast accuracy from tradeable directional edge: improved vol forecasts identify high-uncertainty regimes that inform position sizing and risk management but do not directly generate directional alpha in Gold futures. We document the conditions under which GVZ signals function as regime context rather than directional triggers, and discuss implications for systematic Gold trading strategies.

title: Trading the Volatility Risk Premium on Nifty 50: Strategy Backtest with Realistic Frictions

detail.title: Trading the Volatility Risk Premium on Nifty 50: Strategy Backtest with Realistic Frictions
detail.abstract: Systematic sellers of variance risk on U.S. equity index options have long earned a positive risk premium, but whether that premium survives realistic transaction costs in an emerging market with a high Securities Transaction Tax (STT) and wide bid-ask spreads remains an open question. This paper tests four short-volatility strategies on Nifty 50 index options over 119 monthly expiry cycles from January 2015 to April 2025, applying a cost model that incorporates STT (0.05% on sell-side premium), brokerage (0.03% per leg), slippage (0.5% of premium), and, for the deltahedged variant, daily futures rebalancing costs (0.01% per trade). The four strategies examined are an ATM short straddle, a crash-neutral spread, a naked put-write at four moneyness levels (k = 0.94, 0.96, 0.98, 1.00), and a delta-hedged straddle. Net of all costs, every strategy produces negative annualized returns. The put-write at k = 0.94 is the least adverse outcome, with a 91.6% monthly win rate and an annualized return of-0.9% (Sharpe ratio-0.37); the straddle variants lose approximately 44 to 45% per year. Cost attribution confirms that transaction costs are a secondary factor; the primary driver of losses across all strategies is tail risk, with single-month drawdowns reaching-13.2% of margin for the straddle variants and-18.3% for the k = 0.98 put-write (Table 1). These findings imply that the volatility risk premium documented in Pillai (2026a) exists in Indian index options but is not capturable by a retail trader under current market microstructure.

detail.abstract: Large language models are collapsing the marginal cost of producing a patent application, shifting the binding constraint for individual inventors from professional drafting to the throughput of the filing office. We use a documented existence proof — one inventor filing 75 applications with a single office over 96 days using a two-model AI pipeline — to structure a forward-looking analysis of the consequences for patent systems. Drawing on the verified trace of that deployment, we argue the most immediate effects are not doctrinal questions about machine inventorship but practical pressures: a redistribution of office workload toward formalities and correspondence (the office issued substantive notices on only 8% of applications, while a self-inflicted configuration error propagated to 27%); new disclosure and prior-art-integrity questions raised by human-directed, machine-drafted volume; the dual use of automation for defensive disclosure and offensive thickets (41% of applications were cross-linked); an unresolved distributional question about who benefits; and a novel, correlated failure mode in which one setup error replicates across a portfolio. We set out a neutral menu of policy options, much of it observable in offices' own administrative data, and discuss the limits of reasoning from a single case.

title: Beyond Technological Convergence: ESG Discourse Dominance and Channel-Conditional Emotional Framing in Mega-Capitalized Corporate Reports (2024-2025)

detail.title: Beyond Technological Convergence: ESG Discourse Dominance and Channel-Conditional Emotional Framing in Mega-Capitalized Corporate Reports (2024-2025)

detail.abstract:
Background: The post-2024 commercialization of generative artificial intelligence (AI) and the concurrent tightening of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) regulatory regimes have created competing institutional pressures on corporate disclosure. The relative dominance of these competing narratives, and the extent to which their emotional framing differs across communication channels, remains empirically contested. Objectives: This study identifies the dominant institutional narrative in mega-capitalized corporate discourse and tests whether emotional valence differs systematically between financial and ESG reporting channels. 
Methods: Quantitative content analysis combined with automated sentiment analysis (TextBlob) was conducted on 290 corporate documents from publicly traded firms (market capitalization > USD 100 billion) published 2024-2025. Methodological controls included word-boundary regular-expression matching, NLTK Punkt sentence tokenization, document-length normalization (mentions per 1,000 words), and content-based report-type classification. Inferential testing used one-way ANOVA, Welch's ttest (unequal variances), and chi-square, with effect sizes reported as Cohen's d, Cramér's V, and etasquared.
 Findings: Contrary to prevailing assumptions of AI-driven discursive dominance, ESG language emerged as the most frequent institutional narrative (M = 1.55 mentions per 1,000 words; SD = 2.74), exceeding technological references (M = 1.19; SD = 1.89) and traditional firm-centric narratives (Supply Chain Resilience M = 0.50; Shareholder Primacy M = 0.49). All four narratives appeared in 83-95% of documents, indicating broad coexistence rather than singular convergence. Emotional valence diverged significantly by report type: ESG reports were systematically more positive than financial filings (M = 0.073 vs. M = 0.053; Welch t =-6.15, p < .001, Cohen's d =-0.82). This asymmetry persisted for technology-specific sentiment (Cohen's d =-0.66). Chi-square testing confirmed that report type and valence category are statistically dependent (χ² = 24.24, p < .001, Cramér's V = 0.29). 
Conclusions: ESG-not technology-is the dominant institutional discourse in mega-capitalized corporate communication during 2024-2025. The communication paradox manifests not through lexical convergence on AI vocabulary but through channel-conditional emotional framing, in which firms modulate emotional valence to meet differential stakeholder expectations. These results challenge a widespread assumption about AI-era corporate disclosure and suggest that ESG regulatory pressure has produced stronger institutional convergence than the generative-AI hype cycle.

title: Data-Driven Transfer Evaluation in the Bundesliga: A Production Function Analysis of FC Augsburg's Transfer Efficiency 2021–2024

detail.title: Data-Driven Transfer Evaluation in the Bundesliga: A Production Function Analysis of FC Augsburg's Transfer Efficiency 2021–2024
detail.abstract: This paper examines the transfer efficiency of FC Augsburg, a mid-table Bundesliga club, across three seasons from 2021 to 2024. Using a Weighted Attacking Production Index(WAPI) grounded in the Expected Threat framework of Singh (2018), we evaluate the attacking contribution per euro of transfer fee for all incoming signings with sufficient playing time. An OLS regression across a six-club panel (n = 18) indicates that gross transfer expenditure explains only 2.7% of Bundesliga points variance (p = 0.516), while defensive stability explains 55.1% when included as a co-predictor (p = 0.001). Analysis of individual signings reveals that Augsburg’s most expensive permanent acquisitions—Ricardo Pepi (€16.36M) and Niklas Dorsch (€7M) — delivered the lowest WAPI value scores in the dataset, while the highest-value acquisition (Mergim Berisha, €300K loan) produced 384 times more WAPI per euro than Pepi. Three illustrative counterfactual scenarios, drawn from the 2. Bundesliga and adjusted for league strength following Laseketal. (2013),demonstrate normalised WAPI improvements of 6.2 to 13.9 times at aggregate fee savings of €18.86 million. The findings suggest that positional allocation of spend — rather than expenditure volume — is the primary driver of transfer efficiency at mid-table level, and that publicly available data is sufficient to identify meaningful market inefficiencies prior to transfer decisions.

detail.abstract: Patent portfolios range from heaps of unrelated inventions to architectures whose components reference and reinforce one another. Architecture is normally a firm-scale, deliberately resourced achievement. We examine a portfolio of 75 applications filed by a single inventor over 96 days using AI-assisted drafting, in which 41% of applications carry explicit cross-cluster relationships and one cluster pair exhibits a systematic parent–child mapping between energy (vehicle-to-grid) inventions and corresponding post-quantum-security inventions, including named but unfilled gaps. We define architectural coherence by analogy with modularity and architectural innovation, document it at the portfolio and cluster-pair levels, and argue — against the narrative of spontaneous machine emergence — that the coherence is best understood as human architectural intent executed cheaply by an AI pipeline. The broader implication is that AI-assisted drafting may move portfolio architecture from a firm-scale to an individual-scale capability, with consequences for how portfolio structure is read and for what the empirical study of innovation should measure. We discuss the limits of inferring structure from a single, inventor-coded portfolio.

detail.title: How Labor Market Competition Shapes Workplace Information on Social Media: Evidence from Glassdoor Reviews

declarations.funderStatement: Li acknowledges funding from Shanghai Pujiang Program (25PJC047). Wang acknowledges funding from the Lee Kong Chian Fellowship, the Ministry of Education’s (MOE) Academic Research Fund (AcRF) (22-SOA-SMU-032), and MOE’s Tier 2 Research Grant (MOE-T2EP40124-0007). Zhang acknowledges funding from the Lee Kong Chian Professorship at Singapore Management University.

detail.abstract: We examine how labor market competition affects the quality of workplace information on social media. Using employer reviews on Glassdoor for U.S. publicly listed firms from 2011 to 2022, we find that reviews become less informative about actual workplace practices when firms face more intense competition for labor, consistent with competition inducing workplace information management. The decline in review informativeness is more pronounced when employees have narrower external networks, when firms are less unionized, and when firms have a smaller review base, suggesting that workplace information management is more likely when labor market information asymmetry is greater. Additional analyses show that positive reviews in highly competitive labor markets predict higher short-term labor inflows but greater subsequent employee turnover, indicating a systematic gap between managed expectations and actual workplace conditions. Taken together, our evidence suggests that labor market competition potentially distorts the crowdsourced signals available to job seekers on anonymous review platforms, highlighting an important source of information frictions in the labor market.

title: Sectoral Economic Efficiency and National Growth: A Novel Multi-Dimensional Framework with International Panel Evidence Across Development Stages

detail.title: Sectoral Economic Efficiency and National Growth: A Novel Multi-Dimensional Framework with International Panel Evidence Across Development Stages

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests, personal relationships, or affiliations that could have influenced the work reported in this study. No conflicts of interest are declared.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patients, or personally identifiable data requiring formal ethics committee approval. Where applicable, only publicly available or secondary data sources were used.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The study was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
Understanding which economic sectors deliver the highest return to cost remains a fundamental, unresolved question in development economics and macroeconomic policy design. Existing cost-benefit frameworks are often sector-specific, theoretically inadequate, or analytically static; they fail to capture the dynamic, phase-dependent nature of sectoral productivity. This paper presents a novel, multidimensional Sectoral Economic Productivity Index (SEEI) and, based on it, proposes the Sectoral Productivity Frontier Theory (SEFT), a formal theoretical framework that posits that optimal sectoral investment priorities are neither universal nor static, but systematically dependent on a country's stage of economic development, institutional capacity, and inter-sectoral complementarity apparatus. Furthermore, we derive the Dynamic Cost-Benefit Productivity Index (DCBPI), which extends the SEEI to capture risk-adjusted, horizon-specific productivity across short-term (1-3 years), medium-term (3-10 years), and long-term (10+ years) horizons.

SEEI is constructed as a ratio of a composite Benefit Index, encompassing GDP growth contribution, job creation, labor productivity growth, export performance, and innovation output, to a composite Cost Index, which includes capital investment requirements, public financial support, environmental costs, impact duration, and infrastructure requirements; a diffusion multiplier, capturing cross-sectoral linkage density, has also been added to this index. The index is applied to a balanced international panel dataset covering 127 countries, built using coordinated data from the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, the OECD, the International Labour Organization, UNIDO, and the World Intellectual Property Organization, covering the period 1995–2023.

Employing Fixed Effects, Random Effects, Dynamic Panel System GMM (Blundell-Bond), Difference-in-Differences, and Quantile Regression estimators, we find robust empirical support for all four core propositions of SEFT. Information and communication technology (ICT) and advanced business services generate the highest SEEI in high-income economies (β = 0.241, p < 0.001 at the 90th growth quantile), while advanced manufacturing and industrial upgrading yield superior efficiency gains in upper-middle-income economies. Infrastructure investment provides a universally high short-run SEEI across development stages. In the long run, R&D-intensive sectors, the green energy transition, and education-linked human capital formation dominate the efficiency frontier, with DCBPI values approximately 2.4 to 3.1 times higher than short-run comparators. Results are robust to alternative weighting schemes, instrument proliferation controls, subsample analysis, and placebo tests.

The findings generate directly applicable policy implications: Economies maximize aggregate productivity not by choosing a single sectoral leader, but by prioritizing investments according to a phased portfolio of productivity; first infrastructure, then ICT-manufacturing co-investment, followed by knowledge and green economy foundations. These results provide a new empirical basis for rethinking industrial policy design, particularly for middle-income economies undergoing structural transformation under fiscal constraints.

title: SEER: Self-Equation Extractor & Recognizer Symbolic Recovery of Feedback Functions in Algorithmic Trading Signals

detail.title: SEER: Self-Equation Extractor & Recognizer Symbolic Recovery of Feedback Functions in Algorithmic Trading Signals

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study relies entirely on the computational analysis of publicly available historical market data and synthetic simulation models, involving no human or animal participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: We introduce SEER (Self-Equation Extractor & Recognizer), a symbolic regression pipeline for identifying the functional form of feedback relationships between algorithmic trading signals and subsequent price returns. An MLP forecaster produces a signal U (t) from market features; SEER uses PySR [1] to recover the unknown feedback function f such that Y (t + 1) = g(X(t)) + f (U (t)) + ε(t), without assuming linearity. Causal identification is guaranteed by construction under controlled synthetic injection: ground-truth coefficients are sealed prior to fitting and verified via SHA-256 hash. We evaluate SEER on BTC/USD hourly data (2022-2024, ∼17,500 observations) across six injection regimes-linear, quadratic, sinusoidal, hidden product interaction, asymmetric (ReLU-type), and confounded-and benchmark it against OLS, Lasso, and Random Forest. SEER recovers non-linear feedback structures with coefficient errors below 2% where linear baselines fail entirely (R 2 < 0.01). On unmanipulated market data, no feedback signal is detected above the noise floor (λ ≈ 2.2 × 10-5), consistent with the known negligibility of retail-scale market impact at hourly resolution [3, 9, 15]; this constitutes a negative control rather than a novel empirical finding. Key limitations include restriction to stationary, single-agent settings and the controlled nature of the injection framework. Reproducible Kaggle notebooks accompany this paper [16, 17].

title: A Theory of Sequential Decision Making
affiliations: Universita di Chieti Pescara

detail.title: A Theory of Sequential Decision Making
detail.abstract: This paper develops a theory of sequential decision-making in which the organisation of evidence is an endogenous object of choice. Before evaluation begins, an agent selects a sign-coherent partition of the state space and orders its blocks by the strength of their payo¤-relevant content. The resulting representational structure governs how rapidly decisive evidence accumulates during sequential evaluation and therefore shapes both the speed and reliability of the decision procedure. The paper studies this problem across three complementary environments: an exogenous representational-capacity constraint, a per-block attention cost, and a one-time acquisition cost amortised over repeated evaluations. The analysis characterises structural conditions governing admissible representations, introduces a partial ordering of evaluative structures by their joint performance in evidential concentration and payo¤ discrimination, and studies the trade-o¤ between these two dimensions. Under costly evaluation, distinctions are resolved selectively, with local thresholds determined by the ratio of envelope cost to discriminatory gain. Under repeated use, investment in sequential decision structures is governed by reuse value-the product of decision frequency and stakes-generating endogenous heterogeneity in representational re…nement across agents and domains; frequency and stakes are not separately identi…ed from the acquired structure. The paper further identi…es evaluative environments in which coarse representations are globally optimal, environments in which …ner representations dominate, and alignment environments in which the same representation jointly improves evidential concentration and payo¤ discrimination. The speed-accuracy trade-o¤ is therefore conditional not only on the stopping threshold, but also on the evaluative structure through which evidence is organised prior to inspection.

title: Reversing the Herd: Binding Caps and the Direction of Innovation
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), Anderson School of Management, Students

detail.title: Reversing the Herd: Binding Caps and the Direction of Innovation
detail.abstract: Firms rarely search across the full technological landscape, often herding around narrow, familiar trajectories. Prior work attributes this to incentives arising from a feedback loop of positive market signals and deepening firm investments. Less is known, however, about what happens when these incentives are exogenously cut off or reduced without rendering the underlying knowledge obsolete. This paper studies the European Union's 2014 wattage cap on vacuum cleaners, an industry in which decades of competition had concentrated innovation around increasing motor power. Using a difference-indifferences design based on firms' pre-policy EU patent filing shares, I find no detectable decline in overall patenting, but a significant increase in the breadth of EU-exposed firms' innovation portfolios. This response is strongest among firms with deeper pre-policy commitments to the constrained trajectory, and appears to operate primarily through the redeployment of existing inventors. This suggests that herding does not necessarily lead to competence traps. In fact, the deep commitments that reinforce exploitation and herding can be leveraged for exploration once that trajectory is capped. Binding caps can therefore be an effective way to reverse innovation herding without picking a new direction, weakening the returns to the existing trajectory and encouraging firms to redeploy accumulated capabilities into adjacent domains.

title: Institutional Constraints on PPP Delivery in Bangladesh: Governance, Risk Allocation, and the Path to Reform

detail.title: Institutional Constraints on PPP Delivery in Bangladesh: Governance, Risk Allocation, and the Path to Reform
detail.abstract: Public-Private Partnerships have become a strategic instrument for addressing Bangladesh's infrastructure financing gap and supporting its Vision 2041 agenda. Despite an expanding pipeline of over 80 projects valued at approximately USD 30 billion, the transition from project identification to financial closure remains persistently slow. Prior scholarship has examined Bangladesh's PPP landscape across policy, legal, and sectoral dimensions, yet the institutional mechanisms sustaining this execution gap remain theoretically underexplored. This study applies institutional theory to explain why delivery failures persist despite a formally adequate framework, drawing on three core concepts: formal and informal institutions, path dependency, and institutional isomorphism. Using a qualitative approach combining document analysis, comparative international review, and practitioner insights from the Bangladesh Planning Commission, BEZA, and the Dhaka Bypass Expressway project, it identifies three mechanisms driving the execution gap. First, path-dependent appraisal norms have embedded inadequate project preparation as a persistent feature of the system. Second, a gap between formal and informal institutions leaves contractual risk allocation unresolved in practice, as agencies defer, renegotiate, or circumvent formal obligations through informal workarounds. Third, isomorphic adoption has delivered international PPP architecture without the coordination practices that make it work: form has travelled, function has not. Comparative evidence from Australia, India, and China grounds a sequenced reform framework targeting all three mechanisms. The paper offers two contributions to PPP governance literature: a theoretically grounded explanation of why execution gaps persist, and a reform pathway that addresses not only formal institutional deficiencies but the informal coordination failures that formal frameworks alone cannot fix.

detail.abstract: Between 2024 and 2026, the AI agent developer toolchain split into eight specialized infrastructure layers, capturing over $13 billion in combined funding. title: Deep Uncertainty Estimation and Decision Support for Construction: MCMC-Based Bayesian Inference and Deep Uncertainty Analysis Approach
affiliations: Umeå University, Harbin Institute of Technology, George Mason University and Harbin Institute of Technology

detail.title: Deep Uncertainty Estimation and Decision Support for Construction: MCMC-Based Bayesian Inference and Deep Uncertainty Analysis Approach

keywords: Markov Chain Monte Carlo-Based Bayesian Inference

detail.abstract: Forecasting future states often relies on reliable prior knowledge and well-specified future conditions. However, this approach becomes increasingly inadequate under current construction conditions. Recent construction planning and operation adopt more new technologies, alongside growing project complexity. This often leads to uncertainties in prior knowledge of construction parameters, processes (parameter uncertainty) and possible future conditions a project might face (scenario uncertainty). This situation, so-called deep uncertainty, makes construction performance estimation and decision-making particularly challenging. An integrated approach is proposed tailored for construction under deep uncertainty. Its core contribution lies in leveraging real-time construction information to complement unclear prior probabilities in uncertainty estimation and support decisions considering uncertain futures. Specifically, MCMC-based Bayesian inference continuously updates performance estimation when prior probabilities are not well defined, integrated by a Deep Uncertainty analysis to inform effective construction decisions under plausible future conditions. A field study of a super-high-rise project, validated via simulated execution, showed improvements of 8.57% in duration and 1.67% in cost relative to projects without proposed approach, outperforming random and repeated adjustment practices. This is a theoretical advance regarding how separate uncertainty estimation and decision support should interact in terms of data and process, as a systematic framework to address deep uncertainty in construction.

title: To What Extent Does Fiscal Capacity Influence Infrastructure Delivery Performance? Evidence from Smart Cities Mission Implementation Across Fiscally Diverse Indian Cities

detail.title: To What Extent Does Fiscal Capacity Influence Infrastructure Delivery Performance? Evidence from Smart Cities Mission Implementation Across Fiscally Diverse Indian Cities

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known financial or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based exclusively on publicly available secondary data from government reports, municipal records, and official publications. No human participants were involved, and ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: The Smart Cities Mission (SCM), launched in India in 2015 and formally concluded in March 2025, represents one of the largest centrally sponsored urban infrastructure programmes in the country's history. A common assumption embedded in urban development policy is that fiscally stronger cities-those with higher own-revenue generation and lower grant dependence-deliver better infrastructure outcomes. This paper examines that assumption using data from twelve fiscally diverse Smart Cities Mission cities. Municipal fiscal capacity indicators are drawn from cityfinance.in for financial year 2022-23, while delivery performance is measured through project completion rates sourced from official government publications and parliamentary records. The analysis suggests that fiscal capacity may not be a reliable predictor of delivery outcomes within this sample. Cities across the fiscal spectrum-from Varanasi, with an own-revenue ratio of 28.38 per cent, to Surat, at 74.22 per cent-recorded full or near-complete project delivery. Conversely, two of the fiscally stronger cities in the sample-Chennai and Visakhapatnam-appear to have recorded lower delivery than their fiscal profiles might suggest. The Pearson correlation coefficient between fiscal capacity and project completion across the twelve cities is 0.10, indicating no clear linear relationship within this sample. The paper proposes that delivery performance under centrally sponsored schemes may be more closely associated with administrative capacity, political salience, and project complexity than with municipal fiscal strength. These findings carry implications for the design and evaluation of future urban infrastructure programmes in India.

title: Wasta as Informal Governance: A Componential and Institutional Theory for Emerging Market Economies
affiliations: Assistant Professor, Department of Management, College of Business Administration, Prince Mohammad Bin Fahd University, 617, Al Jawharah, Khobar, Dhahran 34754, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia

detail.title: Wasta as Informal Governance: A Componential and Institutional Theory for Emerging Market Economies
detail.abstract:
Wasta is a social network based on family, lineage, tribe, and extended family. It is used to secure jobs, contracts, promotions, and access to services that are otherwise difficult to obtain. The authors believe that Wasta is not simply a cultural practice or social network but an ingrained broader cognitive model and institutional framework that shapes how people evaluate justice, responsibility, & moral action. Wasta illustrates a cultural mode of mental reasoning in honor-based, relational, interdependent societies where cognition is holistic, and decision-making prioritizes network-based trust, obligation, & loyalty over impartial rules. Wasta in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region and other collectivist societies—in general understood by scholars as the use of personal relationships to secure advantages—remains insufficiently researched, despite its pervasive influence across formal organisational systems and governance in emerging markets. Existing research often treats the Wasta phenomenon as a fragmented concept, often combined with nepotism or favouritism, thereby limiting Wasta measurement, analytical clarity and conceptualization. This research study analysis develops the Componential and Institutional Wasta Theory (CIWT), a multidimensional framework that conceptualizes Wasta as an informal governance mechanism ingrained in institutional and socio-cultural dynamics. Drawing on qualitative evidence from observations, focus groups, interviews, and prior literature, the examination identifies five critical core elements (i.e., factors or roots) that structure Wasta practices and illustrates their differential influence on organisational performance and outcomes, including creativity, innovation, corruption, institutional trust, and employee well-being. The proposed Wasta theoretical framework extends prior studies and advances the literature in five ways: (1) the theoretical framework provides researchers with a unified and agreed-on theoretical definition of Wasta, (2) it explains how institutions create dependence on informal systems (Wasta), and (3) it explains why cognition makes informal systems socially legitimate and self-reinforcing. (4) It presents a measurable componential structure promoting future empirical analysis, and (5) it links informal Wasta practices to formal organisational or institutional performance. By explaining, describing, and clarifying how Wasta functions across formal and informal business and social contexts, the newly developed theory and its theoretical framework offer actionable insights for policymakers, business leaders, and other NGO organizations striving to mitigate bribery, inequality, and corruption and reinforce governance in emerging market economies.

Keywords: Wasta; Informal Governance Mechanisms; Institutional Dynamics; Socio-cultural Dynamics; Wasta Theories; Cognition Theories.

title: Delaware's Living Fossil: Minority Detriment in the Age of SB 21

detail.title: Delaware's Living Fossil: Minority Detriment in the Age of SB 21
detail.abstract:
Delaware Senate Bill 21 (SB 21) generated significant discussion surrounding conflict transactions, including whether the Delaware legislature intended to overrule Sinclair Oil Corp. v. Levien. In Sinclair, the Delaware Supreme Court held that a controlling stockholder engages in self-dealing when it obtains a benefit to the exclusion of, and detriment to, minority stockholders. Although Delaware courts have not consistently invoked Sinclair, this article argues that, prior to SB 21, minority detriment nonetheless remained an essential element of a viable controller self-dealing claim. In particular, this article contends that two recent, pre-SB 21 Delaware Supreme Court decisions confirmed that minority detriment remains necessary to establish self-dealing.

This article next considers whether SB 21 overruled Sinclair. SB 21 added a definition of “controlling stockholder transaction.” Although that definition does not expressly incorporate a minority detriment requirement, this article argues that SB 21 did not overrule Sinclair. SB 21’s legislative history and the Delaware Supreme Court’s subsequent reliance on Sinclair in upholding SB 21’s constitutionality strongly suggest that SB 21 was not intended to expand what constitutes controller self-dealing. This interpretation is consistent with Delaware law’s historic view that the purpose of controller fiduciary duties is minority protection rather than merely to police potential divergent interests.

title: EIZTA: An End-to-End Zero-trust Architecture for Securing High-stakes Offline Examinations in India

detail.title: EIZTA: An End-to-End Zero-trust Architecture for Securing High-stakes Offline Examinations in India
detail.abstract: India's high-stakes public examinations-most notably NEET-UG-have been repeatedly crippled by question-paper leaks and organized fraud that rob millions of candidates of a fair shot. Legal deterrence (culminating in the Public Examinations Act, 2024) and tighter logistics have not stopped the recurrence, because they treat symptoms rather than the underlying architectural failures. This paper introduces EIZTA (Exam Integrity Zero-Trust Architecture)-a five-layer system-level design grounded in an empirically derived 7-gap loop threat model. The architecture integrates Shamir's Secret Sharing for distributed key management, Centre-Level Secure Printing Terminals that eliminate bulk transport of readable papers, per-candidate forensic watermarking, a National Exam Fraud Intelligence Unit (NEFIU) for network-level investigation, and an Independent Exam Security Authority (IESA) for statutory oversight. EIZTA is the first integrated zero-trust lifecycle architecture for high-volume offline examinations in a developing-country context.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Business Ethics and Leadership, volume 9, issue 4, 2025[10.61093/bel.9(4).57-66.2025]

detail.abstract: As organizations accelerate the adoption and use of artificial intelligence, a common misconception arises that equates automation with progress and strategic necessity. This paper argues that not all that can be automated should be automated. It introduces Strategic Minimalism, a disciplined and ethically grounded approach to AI adoption that values purpose, proportionality, and prudence over speed and scale. Drawing on bounded rationality, virtue ethics, and frugal innovation, the study reframes technological restraint as a form of higher intelligence and responsible governance. Methodologically, the framework emerges from a structured conceptual synthesis and abductive reasoning process: the three traditions are integrated into two core dimensions (automation intensity and retained human judgment), whose intersection yields four strategic quadrants (Virtuous Minimalism, Balanced Synergy, Automation Excess, and Performative Minimalism). The framework is then conceptually stress-tested against rival explanations and boundary conditions to ensure internal coherence and analytic validity. By classifying automation into necessary, excessive, and performative types, the paper advances Responsible AI scholarship by identifying restraint as a strategic virtue that strengthens accountability, human oversight, and organizational resilience. Ultimately, it contends that in the age of intelligent machines, leadership wisdom lies not in automating more, but in knowing precisely when and why to stop.
