detail.title: Between Hype and Ambivalence: The Governance of Criminal Justice AI in Africa

publicationDetails.detailsText: Pamela Ugwudike et al (eds) The Oxford Handbook of Digital Technologies in Criminal Justice (Oxford University Press, 2026).

detail.abstract: Imperatives of governing artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly drawing attention in Africa. This is reflected primarily in the adoption of AI strategies at the national and regional levels. In the past few years, over a dozen African countries have issued national AI strategies. The African Union (AU) launched a continental AI strategy as well as a digital compact as part of the AI governance drive in Africa. A handful of countries on the continent have since charted a process towards AI legislation. Drawing upon a case study of national and regional governance initiatives, this chapter explores the extent to which criminal justice AI is governed in Africa. The chapter argues that, clouded by the hype around the economic benefits of AI, the uses of AI in the criminal justice sector are yet to find meaningful attention in emergent AI governance initiatives. Neither the role of AI in modernising criminal justice efforts nor risks of misuse are sufficiently articulated in national and continental AI governance initiatives. The chapter further considers the limits of governance regimes that predate the advent of AI, such as data protection law, in filling the regulatory vacuum. The chapter closes with a caution against the rush to deploy AI systems in criminal justice in the face of such a vacuum, prevalent digital divide and digital illiteracy in the continent. African policymakers must move beyond the traps of hype and regulatory ambivalence.

title: When Stackelberg Leaders Act Like Uncontested Monopolists
affiliations: Stanford University, Yale University and University of Oxford - Department of Economics

detail.title: When Stackelberg Leaders Act Like Uncontested Monopolists
detail.abstract: We show that for a wide class of demand functions in the classic oligopoly games, Stackelberg leaders and uncontested monopolists choose the same actions. By classic oligopoly games we mean both pure complements price competition with heterogeneous constant marginal costs and pure substitutes quantity (Cournot) competition with zero marginal costs. We characterize the class of all demand functions which make the best response of price setters or quantity setters affine in the competitor's simultaneous action. Examples include linear, log-linear, constant elasticity, and power demand curves, encompassing markets with either strategic complements or strategic substitutes. We prove that when the best response is affine, monopolists and Stackelberg leaders do the same thing.

detail.title: Consumer Law and Competition Law

publicationDetails.detailsText: Amsterdam Centre for European Law and Governance Research Paper No. 2026-01

detail.abstract: This chapter analyzes the intersection of these two legal fields in the EU by focusing on their distinct goals, scope, and the legal obligations they impose, while also highlighting how they reinforce each other to provide consumers access to a range of competitively priced goods and services in markets free of unfair and deceptive practices. Several key concepts intersect both fields. The normative construction of the consumer, economic power asymmetries, theories of harm, exploitation, and evolving consumer identities are increasingly relevant, yet analytically challenging, in both fields. These issues gain particular significance in light of contemporary global challenges, including digitalization, climate change, increasing corporate and political concentration, and widening social and economic inequalities. As globalization, climate deterioration and digitalization are profoundly reshaping economic activities, rendering markets more interconnected and complex, this transformation raises cross-cutting challenges, including rising market concentration, data-driven business models, privacy concerns, and exploitative or manipulative consumer strategies. These developments emphasize the need for closer coordination and more systematic synergies between competition and consumer protection policies. The cross-cutting nature of these challenges require a deeper understanding and analysis of how social and economic challenges emerge in markets and how consumer protection and competition law could address these. Against this background, this chapter analyses how these intersecting concepts could improve their capacity to address emerging forms of economic power in modern societies.

title: External Debt Management and Macroeconomic Stability in Developing Countries

detail.title: External Debt Management and Macroeconomic Stability in Developing Countries
detail.abstract: The mounting burden of external debt represents one of the most pressing macroeconomic challenges confronting developing countries in the post-pandemic era. By 2024, the total external debt stock of low-and middle-income countries reached a record US$8.9 trillion, with debt service costs diverting critical public resources away from health, education, and infrastructure investment. This paper examines the relationship between external debt management and macroeconomic stability in developing countries, drawing on recent empirical literature, data from the World Bank International Debt Report (2025), and analysis published by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF). The study analyzes four dimensions of macroeconomic stability-economic growth, inflation, exchange rate dynamics, and fiscal sustainability-and evaluates how the level, composition, and management of external debt affects each. Key findings from the literature confirm a nonlinear "debt-Laffer curve" relationship: moderate external borrowing can support growth by supplementing domestic savings, but excessive debt accumulation triggers debt overhang, crowds out investment, fuels inflationary pressures, and exposes currencies to depreciation spirals. The paper further highlights that institutional quality significantly mediates the debt-growth nexus, and that the post-2022 global monetary tightening cycle has substantially increased refinancing costs for developing economies. Policy recommendations emphasize fiscal consolidation, debt transparency, diversification of creditor bases, and structural reforms to strengthen debt-carrying capacity.

detail.title: Rolling Up Labor: Private Equity, Antitrust, and Labor

detail.abstract: Private equity-backed serial acquisitions, commonly known as "rollups", now account for a significant share of U.S. M&A and are reshaping major industries, from healthcare to software. While scholars and regulators have increasingly scrutinized the consumer-welfare effects of rollups, the effects on labors have received far less attention. This Essay fills that gap and makes five contributions. First, it identifies fragmentation, local or segmented competition, and human-capital intensity as key features of the labor markets commonly targeted by rollups. These features make rollups profitable for PE firms, but they also leave workers especially vulnerable to consolidation. Second, it shows how rollups can depress wages, worsen working conditions, and facilitate anticompetitive coordination among employers. Third, it explains why labor market-specific features-including noncompetes, no-solicitation agreements, and variation in workers' relationship with the company-can magnify these harms. Fourth, it identifies doctrinal and practical obstacles that private plaintiffs and government enforcers face under existing antitrust law. Fifth, given the limits of private litigation and ex post remedies, it offers specific recommendations to strengthen ex ante government enforcement.

title: Autonomous AI and PEs

detail.title: Autonomous AI and PEs

publicationDetails.detailsText: Tax Notes International, Volume 122 No. 7. Pp. 1035-1046

detail.abstract:
The permanent establishment concept of Article 5 of the OECD Model Tax Convention, the gateway to source-country taxation of foreign business income, rests on a foundational assumption that autonomous artificial intelligence has rendered untenable: that income-generating activity is always traceable to a human agent operating through a fixed, tangible location. When an AI system autonomously generates legal opinions, executes trades, or delivers professional services across dozens of jurisdictions without human intervention in any individual transaction, the three-prong test of Article 5 (the place of business test, the fixation test, and the business activity test) fails at each step. There is no tangible installation, no stable geographical link, and no human agent in the source jurisdiction to whom the activity can be attributed. The result is the structural undertaxation of AI-generated income: the source countries that host and sustain its economic effects receive nothing in return.

This paper consolidates a four-part series published in Tax Notes International and makes three contributions. First, it analyses how each prong of the Article 5 test fails when autonomous AI is deployed through the prevailing commercial model of API access and distributed inference. Second, it examines the principal reform proposals (the OECD's significant economic presence concept, Pillar One Amount A, the United States net CFC tested income regime, and Pillar Two) and shows that each was designed for a different problem and leaves the source-country nexus gap untouched. Third, it proposes the Autonomous AI Nexus, a targeted modification to Article 5 that replaces physical presence with three functional equivalents (a deployment test, an economic effects test, and an autonomous activity attribution rule), implemented through a Commentary amendment requiring neither new legal categories, nor AI personhood, nor multilateral overhaul. A case study and three stress tests demonstrate the proposal's precision and its resilience to avoidance.

detail.abstract: In this paper we study the impact of data center development on local economic outcomes, especially the local housing market. Using a staggered difference-indifferences design that exploits variation in data center announcement and construction timing, we find that data center development leads to slower growth in local housing prices. Further analysis shows that data center operations increase electricity consumption and prices. In addition, we find little evidence of improvements in employment, establishment formation, or property tax revenue. Consistent with these disamenities, we find a shift toward more shares of lower-income households in these communities after data center establishment. Lastly, we document a significant increase in spreads on utility municipal bonds issued by localities with new data centers. Our findings suggest that data centers may create noticeable negative externalities for their host communities.

detail.abstract: This volume, Fundamentals of Indirect Taxation, is the fourth in the Fundamentals of Taxation series and offers a comprehensive, comparative, and conceptually rigorous exploration of transaction-based taxes. After a general introduction, the book is structured into seven substantive chapters, each dedicated to a major category of transaction tax: (2) Value Added Tax (VAT/GST), (3) Customs Duties (Tariffs), (4) Excise Duties, (5) Environmental or Green Taxes, (6) Digital Services Taxes, (7) Registration Taxes and Other Taxes on the Raising or Transfer of Capital, and (8) Inheritance, Estate and Gift Taxation. Each chapter systematically addresses the rationale, policy objectives, subjective and objective scope, taxable amount, rates, exemptions, administrative obligations, and residual aspects relevant to its subject. The overall aim of this book is to bridge the gap between technical expertise and conceptual understanding, providing both students and practitioners with a clear, accessible, and globally relevant analysis of indirect taxes. The authors employ a comparative methodology, drawing on examples from multiple jurisdictions and referencing international standards, including those of the OECD, IMF, UN and EU. Special attention is paid to the interplay between indirect taxes and broader fiscal, economic and regulatory policies, as well as to the challenges posed by digitalization, globalization and environmental imperatives. The collective authorship underpinning this volume facilitates a multiplicity of perspectives, thereby enriching the analytical depth of the discourse; concurrently, the adoption of a unified editorial methodology ensures coherence and clarity throughout the work. This primer is intended as an essential resource for students, professionals and curious learners, and fosters a common understanding for those engaging with indirect taxation in a global context.

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the market consequences of the Family Grocery and Farmer Relief Act's proposal to break up multi-species meatpackers into single-species firms to lower beef prices. The analysis compares equilibria in a two-firm, two-product Cournot duopolyduopsony model with those in a four-firm, single-product Cournot oligopoly model. detail.title: The Beacon and The Blunder: Critiquing the EACJ's Inconsistent Path to Regional Integration

publicationDetails.detailsText: The Platform Magazine, volume 122,  March Issue

detail.abstract:
The Kenya-European Union Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA), which came into force in July 2024, was hailed as the most ambitious trade agreement between the EU and a developing country, offering duty and quota-free access for Kenyan exports while requiring Kenya to undertake gradual tariff reductions on imports from the EU. For a country whose share in world exports stood at a mere 0.03% in 2021 and where persistent import-export imbalances have strained the shilling, the agreement represented a vital opportunity to expand international trade prospects. However, the EPA’s implementation has been thrown into uncertainty following the EACJ’s ruling in Centre for Law Economics and Policy of East African Integration v Attorney General of Kenya (Application No. 7 of 2024) [2025] EACJ 10.

This paper critically examines that decision and its implications for Kenya’s trade relations with the EU. To understand the full context, the paper traces the EPA’s origins. The agreement was initially negotiated as a bloc-to-bloc arrangement between the EU and all East African Community (EAC) Partner States, requiring ratification by every member to enter into force. This process was frustrated by the reluctance of Partner States to ratify, with Rwanda being the sole exception, largely because all other EAC members (unlike Kenya) are classified as Least Developed Countries (LDCs). As LDCs, they already enjoy duty- and quota-free access to the EU market under special and differential treatment provisions, and thus saw little incentive to open their own markets to EU imports. Consequently, Kenya sought and obtained approval from other Partner States to proceed with bilateral negotiations, culminating in the 2023 signing of the EPA, which remains open to all EAC members under the principle of variable geometry.

The EACJ’s intervention raises fundamental questions about the Court’s approach to regional integration, the principle of variable geometry, and the balance between supranational adjudication and Partner State autonomy. The paper argues that the ruling not only jeopardises a trade agreement that has already delivered tangible benefits to Kenyan and EU traders for over a year, but also creates legal uncertainty that may deter future trade and investment in the region. By situating the Court’s decision within the broader jurisprudence of the EACJ, including its landmark Katabazi ruling and subsequent case law on supremacy and rule of law, the paper assesses whether the Court has struck an appropriate balance between enforcing treaty compliance and respecting the legitimate policy choices of Partner States. Ultimately, the paper contends that while judicial oversight is essential for the rule of law, the EACJ must exercise its powers with due regard for the practical consequences of its decisions on regional economic integration and the livelihoods of citizens who depend on cross-border trade.

title: Assessing Methane Emissions Policy and Climate Commitments in Azerbaijan's Hydrocarbon Economy
affiliations: Economic Research Center (ERC)

detail.title: Assessing Methane Emissions Policy and Climate Commitments in Azerbaijan's Hydrocarbon Economy
detail.abstract: This article examines methane emissions policy and climate commitments in Azerbaijan's hydrocarbon-dependent economy, with particular attention to the oil and gas sector, which accounts for the overwhelming majority of the country's greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Drawing on national emissions data, international climate commitments, policy documents, and independent assessments, the study evaluates Azerbaijan's progress in methane mitigation and its broader energy transition strategy. The analysis highlights the growing discrepancy between Azerbaijan's climate pledges-including its commitments under the Paris Agreement, the Global Methane Pledge, and various international methane reduction initiatives-and the continued expansion of fossil fuel production and exports. The article argues that methane emissions from oil and gas extraction, transmission, venting, flaring, and aging infrastructure remain a major environmental challenge, while limitations in emissions measurement, transparency, and independent verification continue to undermine the credibility of official reporting. Furthermore, the study examines the environmental and economic risks associated with continued hydrocarbon dependence in a country already experiencing increasing climate vulnerability, including rising temperatures, water scarcity, land degradation, and pressure on agricultural systems. The findings suggest that meaningful methane mitigation will require modernization of energy infrastructure, enhanced monitoring and reporting mechanisms, stronger institutional transparency, and a gradual shift toward renewable energy development. Without substantial structural reforms and a credible decarbonization strategy, Azerbaijan risks falling short of its climate objectives while remaining exposed to the long-term economic and environmental costs of hydrocarbon dependence.

title: Machine Learning Failures in Broker-Driven Emerging Markets: Concept Drift, Regime Switching, and Structural Breaks -Evidence from NEPSE Transaction-Level Data

detail.title: Machine Learning Failures in Broker-Driven Emerging Markets: Concept Drift, Regime Switching, and Structural Breaks -Evidence from NEPSE Transaction-Level Data
detail.abstract: Machine learning models have demonstrated strong predictive performance on developed market data, yet their applicability to broker-driven emerging markets remains poorly understood. We evaluate 12 models across five architectural families-including XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, LSTM, GRU, and Transformer-on 57,285,204 transactions from the Nepal Stock Exchange (NEPSE) spanning 902 trading days (2022-2025), using 4-fold expanding walk-forward validation with 20 features comprising 13 technical indicators and seven novel broker microstructure features, including Order Flow Imbalance and broker concentration indices. No model consistently outperforms the Naive Random Walk baseline, which achieves the highest 4-fold average Sharpe ratio (0.511) and outperforms XGBoost (0.351) and all deep learning architectures, with LSTM producing negative average Sharpe (-0.003). Models show meaningful performance in structurally stable regimes-XGBoost achieves Sharpe 0.917 in the zero-break first fold-but universally fail when test windows contain structural breaks, producing negative Sharpe in the three-break third fold. Directional accuracy remains deceptively stable at 57-59% in structurally stable folds, confirming that accuracy alone is insufficient in fat-tailed markets, and no model survives NEPSE's actual transaction costs (∼0.415% per side), with break-even costs not exceeding 0.032% for any model. Using a 3-state Gaussian Hidden Markov Model and PELT structural break detection, we identify five break dates and demonstrate that break count within the test window directly predicts failure severity, providing a measurable mechanism of concept drift, while broker microstructure features offer partial robustness in bear regimes. We propose a regime-gated deployment framework for machine learning practitioners in broker-driven emerging markets.

title: Intellectual Property Protection and Patent Disclosure Delays in China

detail.title: Intellectual Property Protection and Patent Disclosure Delays in China
detail.abstract: We study how the establishment of specialized intellectual property (IP) protection affects the timing of patent disclosure in China. Using a staggered difference-indifferences design that exploits China's 2011 IP protection pilot program-which designated 85 cities as IP protection demonstration zones-we find that IP protection increases the log number of days to patent disclosure by 6.8 percent and raises the probability that disclosure exceeds the 18-month statutory deadline by 5.4 percentage points. These results suggest that stronger legal enforcement of IP rights induces patentees to delay public disclosure, consistent with a model in which applicants strategically time disclosure to exploit improved post-grant protection. Our findings contribute to the debate on whether stronger IP institutions encourage or inhibit knowledge diffusion.

title: Parental Time and Human Capital Formation: Evidence from the Kibbutz Children's Houses

detail.title: Parental Time and Human Capital Formation: Evidence from the Kibbutz Children's Houses
detail.abstract: From their founding until the 1970s, most Israeli kibbutzim raised children in communal homes known as Beit Yeladim ‫ילדים(‬ ‫,)בתי‬ or the bayit. In this system, infants slept apart from their parents under the care of an unrelated caregiver. We provide the first comprehensive account of how communal rearing-a radical alternative to the nuclear family-shapes adult human capital. Combining Israeli registry data with the staggered institutional dissolution of the kibbutz bayit across 72 Artzi-movement kibbutzim, we document a fundamental trade-off in skill formation. Using differencesin-differences and a control function correction for selective exit, we find that communal rearing compressed the education distribution: children of degree-holding parents lost 1.2 years of schooling, while children of less-educated parents gained 1.2 years. For the high-education group, we document a cognitive-income paradox: despite a 0.50 SD drop in psychometric scores, bayit exposure increased adult income by 0.53 SD. This gain is accompanied by a 25-percentage-point increase in the probability of holding a managerial position (equivalently, a 1.12 increase in log odds) and by sorting into socially intensive occupations. A structural decomposition suggests that while communal rearing disrupted the inter-generational transmission of cognitive skill, it fostered a specific bundle of non-cognitive social capital that the modern labor market highly rewards.

title: Syria’s Path Toward International Tax Integration
affiliations: Voyage Consulting

detail.title: Syria’s Path Toward International Tax Integration
detail.abstract:
This study examines Syria’s pathway toward integration into the modern international tax and financial system through institutional reform, OECD alignment, and long-term participation in advanced international economic governance frameworks. The paper argues that Syria’s most strategically important objective at this stage is not the immediate negotiation of bilateral tax treaties, but the formal initiation of a structured process toward engagement with the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and related international standards frameworks.
The timing of this study is particularly significant following Syria’s invitation to participate in the G7 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors meetings in Paris. This development represents an important political and economic opening for Syria to begin both the political and technical process of requesting structured engagement with OECD countries and institutions. The study presents this moment as a rare strategic opportunity to reposition Syria within the international economic system through a credible reform-oriented framework focused on transparency, governance modernization, financial integrity, and institutional reliability.

The paper explains that modern treaty readiness extends far beyond domestic tax reform. Developed economies increasingly evaluate potential treaty and investment partners based on broader institutional credibility, including regulatory transparency, exchange-of-information capability, anti-abuse enforcement, banking-sector governance, anti-money laundering systems, dispute-resolution mechanisms, and participation in internationally recognized frameworks such as the OECD/G20 BEPS initiative, FATF standards, CRS, and EOIR transparency systems.
The study reviews Syria’s recent reform efforts in fiscal policy, tax modernization, banking-sector rehabilitation, financial transparency, and engagement with international financial institutions. While these developments represent important progress, the paper emphasizes that substantial institutional, technical, and governance gaps remain and that long-term credibility will depend on sustained implementation and operational modernization.
Accordingly, the study strongly advises the Syrian finance ministry in coordination with the Syrian ministry of foreign affairs and related governmental institutions to undertake a comprehensive technical review of the frameworks discussed throughout the paper, particularly those relating to OECD standards, BEPS implementation, transfer pricing, exchange-of-information systems, FATCA cooperation, financial transparency, beneficial ownership, and international tax administration infrastructure. These technical components collectively form the operational foundation required for meaningful participation in modern international tax cooperation frameworks.

Ultimately, the study concludes that Syria’s long-term economic integration and investment competitiveness will depend on its ability to establish durable institutional trust, transparent governance systems, and internationally credible administrative capacity. Within this framework, future tax treaties with developed economies should be viewed not as initial objectives, but as outcomes of sustained institutional reform, international alignment, and successful integration into the global financial and economic system.

title: Supply and Allocation in Race-Segmented Marriage Markets: Same-Segment Partnership among College Women in the United States, 1980-2024
affiliations: Liaoning University

detail.title: Supply and Allocation in Race-Segmented Marriage Markets: Same-Segment Partnership among College Women in the United States, 1980-2024
detail.abstract: The college share of U.S. women aged 25–44 rose from 16 to 45 percent between 1980 and 2024. This expansion entered race-segmented marriage markets in which same- segment partnership is a central high-resource matching channel. I introduce an ac- counting framework that decomposes the same-segment high-resource partnership rate of college women, Y = M/W, into the gross supply of same-segment high-resource men, R = H/W, and the realized allocation rate, Q = M/H. The main application is the post-1990 trajectory of Black college women: their same-race high-resource partnership share falls from 0.20 to 0.15, while the gross supply of Black college-educated employed men per Black college woman remains essentially flat at 0.86–0.88 and the allocation rate falls from 0.24 to 0.17. The same pattern holds at the commuting-zone level, in both the 2024 cross-section and within-CZ changes since 1990. The conclusion is robust to composition reweighting and to alternative definitions of the high-resource male stock. Comparative applications clarify other race-segments: Hispanic college women’s high-resource partnership declines mainly through a weakening cross-segment margin, while aggregate Asian stability conceals divergent Indian and Filipino subgroup trajectories.

reference: The University of Chicago Stone Center Working Paper Series Paper No. 26-08
title: The Social Limits of Incentives Embeddedness and the Scope Conditions of Economic Theory
affiliations: Princeton University - Department of Sociology

detail.title: The Social Limits of Incentives Embeddedness and the Scope Conditions of Economic Theory

publicationDetails.detailsText: The University of Chicago Stone Center Working Paper Series Paper No. 26-08
publicationDetails.journalName: The University of Chicago Stone Center Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Economic theory expects individuals to respond decisively to financial incentives, yet empirical research often finds surprisingly small elasticities. This essay argues that such weak effects are often evidence that economic action is mediated by social structure. I develop a framework of socially attenuated incentives in which embeddedness raises the relational, reputational, and identity costs of acting on financial incentives, thereby weakening responsiveness to incentives. Incentives remain important, but their effects are filtered through networks, identities, and norms. Incentive-only models resemble gravity-only physics: accurate in idealized conditions but incomplete in socially dense environments. Small elasticities are often the empirical traces of embeddedness. 

I formalize this argument with a simple model and illustrate it across multiple domains: consumer transactions, tax migration among top earners, and labor supply responses to unemployment insurance. In contrast, private equity buyouts in some sectors demonstrate how profits can be generated by dismantling embedded constraints and intensifying high-powered incentives, a process of disembedding arbitrage. Together, these cases outline a research agenda for economic sociology focused on the social conditions that attenuate or reshape the force of incentives in economic life.

detail.abstract: Since Jan. 1, sell-side analysts have lowered observable energy production expectations by 1.9% (1.5 million boe/d1) while raising energy earnings forecasts by 57% ($227 billion). This divergence signals a market revaluation consistent with a scarcity premium: higher profits despite lower expected output. AI adds a related transmission channel. As AI-linked growth increases demand for energy and other constrained inputs, scarcity in one part of the system can manifest as cost pressure elsewhere. At the same time, broader markets have been comparatively stable over the first five months of 2026.

title: Causal Identification of Renewable Portfolio Standard Effectiveness: Evidence from a Multi-Method Panel Analysis of U.S. State Carbon Intensity, 2001–2022

detail.title: Causal Identification of Renewable Portfolio Standard Effectiveness: Evidence from a Multi-Method Panel Analysis of U.S. State Carbon Intensity, 2001–2022
detail.abstract:
State-level Renewable Portfolio Standards (RPS) are the primary regulatory instrument driving electricity-sector decarbonization in the United States, yet the causal evidence linking mandate stringency to carbon intensity reductions remains contested. This study provides the first integrated five-method empirical evaluation of RPS effectiveness, combining Two-Way Fixed-Effects panel regression with Instrumental Variables (TWFE-IV), staggered Difference-in-Differences with Causal Forest estimation, LSTM neural network forecasting, XGBoost stacking ensemble classification with SHAP interpretability, and regional subgroup analysis across 51 U.S. jurisdictions from 2001 to 2022.

The preferred TWFE-IV specification yields β = −0.00373 (p = .017), confirming that each one-percentage-point increase in renewable share causally reduces CO₂ intensity by 0.0037 tons/MWh. RPS adoption produces a Causal Forest Average Treatment Effect on the Treated of −0.1351 tons/MWh (p < .001). LSTM forecasting reveals near-unit-root CO₂ dynamics (ρ = 0.846), establishing that policy evaluation windows shorter than three to five years are statistically inadequate. The XGBoost ensemble achieves AUC-ROC = 0.968, identifying mandate stringency above 35% as the dominant decarbonization threshold. The West and South deliver 2.3 times the national average decarbonization return per unit of renewable expansion; the Northeast's positive coefficient is attributed to SUTVA violations from interstate electricity trading.

Findings resolve a direct empirical conflict with Novan (2015), whose null CO₂ result is attributable to a pre-2015 panel that predates the cumulative capacity build-out captured here, and with Shrimali and Kniefel (2011), whose weak-effects finding reflects a low-stringency mandate regime that does not generalize above the 35% threshold identified by SHAP.

detail.abstract: This chapter uses vulnerability theory to examine the ideas about government structure behind the rise of neoliberal and illiberal constitutional law, showing how these amplify liberal notions of autonomy and legitimate authority. The liberal ideal of a restrained government comprised of autonomous subjects fuels a politics of despair and division as systemic crises make individual choices increasingly risky and confusing.  Individual constitutional rights get popular attention, but these can only be realized through institutions. The vulnerable subject challenges the structural “common sense” of U.S. liberal political and legal theory by redirecting institutional accountability from the formal individual to the embodied, embedded human being.  This shift highlights human dependence on institutions and strengthens constitutional ground for resisting both neoliberalism and illiberalism. By repositioning the state as a provider of human resilience, rather than facilitator of individual autonomy, vulnerability theory provides a more robust direction for structural analysis and for an affirmative constitutional politics of democracy and social justice.

title: Liquidity Provision of Syndicated Credit Lines
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Liquidity Provision of Syndicated Credit Lines
detail.abstract: ​A large fraction of credit lines to the corporate sector are syndicated allowing for risk-diversification and coinsurance. We develop a simple model to study the provision of liquidity through syndicated credit lines. The capacity of banks to provide liquidity to firms depends on the structure of the interbank network arising from syndication and on a set of interbank commitments called fronting exposures that facilitate payment flows among syndicate members. We show that the liquidity capacity has increased significantly following the introduction of liquidity regulation. Furthermore, the liquidity co-insurance of interbank fronting exposures is economically important for the corporate sector. Finally, we document that borrowers with higher reliance on credit lines have become more likely to obtain credit lines from syndicates with higher liquidity capacities. This assortative matching on liquidity characteristics has strengthened the importance of large banks as liquidity providers to the corporate sector in the post GFC period.

title: The Singularity of Abundance
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Singularity of Abundance
detail.abstract: All existing theories of value-from the classical school to marginalism-rest on the postulate of resource scarcity. This paper introduces the Theory of Abundance Singularity (TAS), a macroeconomic framework analyzing the structural collapse of monetary exchange systems when the marginal cost of producing physical and cognitive goods converges asymptotically to zero due to integral automation. We distinguish rigorously between rival goods (physical resources with binding marginal costs) and non-rival goods (information, software, algorithmic outputs), and define a saturation index φ(t) measuring the GDP share in the zeromarginal-cost regime. We demonstrate that when φ crosses a critical threshold φ*, Fisher's equation of exchange (MV = PT) undergoes a thermodynamic phase transition: monetary circulation velocity V decays toward zero, rendering traditional pricing mechanisms mathematically indeterminate. We derive the velocity decay function from a microeconomic model of agent exchange propensity, introduce the Abundance Saturation Coefficient (ASC) as a measurable macroeconomic indicator, and model consumption as a logistic function with biological and social saturation limits. The framework generates testable predictions about price deflation, velocity collapse, and the emergence of non-monetary allocation mechanisms.

title: Bank Responses to FinTech Disruption: The Role of Innovation Culture
affiliations: SUNY at Albany - School of Business, University of Naples Parthenope - Department of Management Studies and Quantitative Methods, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Milano-Bicocca

detail.title: Bank Responses to FinTech Disruption: The Role of Innovation Culture
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether innovation culture influences banks’ strategic responses to FinTech disruption. We develop a novel AI-based measure of innovation culture using the Business Description, Risk Factors, and MD&A sections of Form 10-K filings for U.S. banks from 2013–2023. The measure captures latent cultural traits and enables firm-year-level analysis across a large panel. We relate innovation culture to banks’ FinTech investments, partnerships, risk-taking, capital adequacy, and stock performance. Banks with stronger innovation cultures are significantly more likely to invest in FinTech startups and form partnerships with FinTech firms. These effects are particularly pronounced among smaller banks, where lower organizational complexity may allow innovation-oriented values to translate more readily into strategic action. Although innovation-oriented banks exhibit modestly higher risk-weighted asset intensity, they maintain capital discipline and do not exhibit greater insolvency risk. Overall, the findings identify organizational culture as an important determinant of banks’ responses to technological disruption.

title: Did GST 2.0 Reduce Classification Disputes, or Relocate Them?
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Did GST 2.0 Reduce Classification Disputes, or Relocate Them?
detail.abstract: India’s “GST 2.0” reform of 22 September 2025 replaced the earlier multi-rate GST structure with two main slabs (5% and 18%) and a 40% rate for demerit goods. The government argued that fewer rates would reduce classification disputes. We test this claim using published Advance Ruling (AAR) and Appellate Advance Ruling (AAAR) decisions. Our key methodological contribution is showing that the GST Council’s advance-ruling portal provides a near-complete, machine-tagged census of roughly 2,940 rulings, enabling direct issue-based analysis. As of May 2026, the evidence supports two findings: (1) it is still too early to conclusively determine whether disputes have fallen because the post-reform dataset remains limited by publication lags; and (2) the available evidence suggests disputes have shifted rather than disappeared. Post-reform rulings continue to contest the 5%–18% boundary, the reform has generated new inverted-duty refund disputes, and authorities have strengthened mechanisms for resolving inter-state conflicts. We provide the coding framework, ruling dataset, statistical methods, and replication protocol needed to reassess the reform’s effects as more post-2025 rulings become available.

detail.title: Trade Consequences of Sanctions: A Systematic Review
detail.abstract: This systematic literature review examines the trade consequences of economic sanctions, a central instrument in contemporary geopolitics with significant implications for global trade flows, networks, and macroeconomic synchronization. The objective is to provide a mechanism-based synthesis of how sanctions reshape international trade. Following PRISMA guidelines, the review analyses 115 peer-reviewed studies and develops an integrated general-equilibrium framework distinguishing the sender, target, and the rest of the world (ROW) while examining four key channels: direct bilateral effects, trade diversion, spillovers, and changes in trade-comovement. Findings reveal that sanctions induce large trade flows contractions through both intensive and extensive margins, trigger trade diversion toward third countries, and generate spillover effects that reconfigure global networks and weaken synchronization of GDP, consumption, and industrial production, with substantial heterogeneity by sanction type, instruments, and sector characteristics. By first focusing on the trade consequences of sanctions, this review addresses a critical gap in earlier broad-scope studies and identifies promising directions for future research.

title: Text-Based ESG Beliefs and Mutual Fund Performance: Evidence from LLM Analysis of Fund Narratives

detail.title: Text-Based ESG Beliefs and Mutual Fund Performance: Evidence from LLM Analysis of Fund Narratives
detail.abstract: ESG beliefs are a key conceptual dimension shaping how investors integrate sustainability into investment decisions. We develop a novel text-based measure of fund managers' ESG-related narrative orientation by applying large language models to the strategy statements and market outlooks in mutual fund reports, and use it as an empirical proxy for managers' underlying ESG beliefs. Stronger ESG-related orientation in these narratives is positively associated with subsequent fund performance, yet investors do not appear to fully price it. The performance gains stem from superior stock selection: managers with stronger orientation overweight firms with higher ESG scores while remaining attentive to fundamentals. The effect is amplified after the carbon neutrality pledge, in favorable markets, and in funds with more institutional investors. Our findings highlight the economic importance of ESG-related managerial heterogeneity  and provide new evidence on how sustainability considerations are incorporated into asset management.

detail.abstract: A material share of signed letters of intent (LOIs) in U.S. private-company mergers and acquisitions (M&A) do not result in closed transactions, but the empirical mix of causes has shifted measurably between 2023 and 2025. Drawing on the 2025 Axial Dead Deal Report (N = 75 unsuccessful transactions), the SRS Acquiom 2025 Working Capital Purchase Price Adjustment Study (N = 1,250 private-target deals, 2020 through Q3 2024), and the academic literature on termination provisions and deal completion, this paper documents three findings. First, diligence-driven failures (non-quality-of-earnings findings and quality-of-earnings EBITDA discrepancies combined) accounted for 46.6% of post-LOI deal failures in 2025, with quality-of-earnings discrepancies roughly doubling from 10.6% in 2023 to 21.3% in 2025. Second, financing-driven failures declined by approximately half over the same window, falling from 21.3% in 2023 to 10.7% in 2025, consistent with easing credit conditions and the increased share of private-equity capital available for lower middle market transactions. Third, retrade dynamics (buyer-initiated post-LOI renegotiation) account for 14.7% of failures and are typically downstream of diligence findings rather than independent causes. The paper situates these findings within the academic literature on termination-fee provisions and deal protection devices (Bates & Lemmon, 2003; Officer, 2003; Boone & Mulherin, 2007), discusses the gap between published large-cap M&A research and the LMM private-company segment, and considers implications for sellers, buyers, and intermediaries. Limitations of small-sample practitioner data and the absence of a deal-level census of private LOIs are addressed.

title: Too Soon to Tell: Statistical Power and the Effect Sizes of Asset Pricing Factors

detail.title: Too Soon to Tell: Statistical Power and the Effect Sizes of Asset Pricing Factors
detail.abstract: This paper prespecifies minimum economically meaningful effect sizes-a Sharpe ratio of 0.3, a compound growth rate of 1% per annum and analogous thresholds for risk-adjusted returns-before applying the Neyman-Pearson framework to a shortlist of well-documented asset pricing factors. Detecting a Sharpe ratio of 0.3 requires 87 years of monthly data for 80% power. Detecting a compound growth rate of 1% per annum requires 234-554 years depending on the factor. No post-publication window approaches these requirements. Not one result qualifies as a non-rejection with adequate power. The replication crisis in asset pricing is partly a power crisis in disguise.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None of the authors has personal of financial relationship with other people or organizations that may have or could be perceived to have influenced this study.

detail.abstract: This paper identifies the aggregate trading of active mutual funds as an economically significant driver of the equity term structure. When funds collectively tilt their portfolios toward short-duration equities, the term structure of forward-looking monthly returns slopes sharply downward for the stocks they purchase most heavily. These tilting episodes are short-lived and dispersed over time, patterns that rule out slow-moving pricing factors. Funds tilting toward short-duration stocks outperform those tilting toward long-duration stocks by 1.8% the following month—but only during tilting periods. Our findings are consistent with equilibrium models in which asset managers are evaluated over short performance windows.

title: Telco and OTT Services: Substitutes or Complements?

detail.title: Telco and OTT Services: Substitutes or Complements?
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether traditional mobile communication services, namely voice and SMS, and over-the-top (OTT) communication services, namely app-based calling and instant messaging, are substitutes or complements. This question is central to relevant market definition and to current regulatory debates on telecom-OTT convergence. The paper contributes by moving the analysis from functional similarity to structural demand substitution. We develop a constant-elasticity-ofsubstitution (CES) framework in which the telecom-to-OTT expenditure ratio responds to a relative user-cost index. To address the zero-price nature of many OTT services, OTT user cost is proxied by the effective mobile-data price required to consume app-based communication services. The model is estimated on a country-quarter panel covering 29 countries from 2017Q3 to 2024Q2, combining operator-level telecom data with app-level OTT usage and data-consumption information. Relativeprice endogeneity is addressed using leave-one-country-out shift-share price shifters and predetermined price variation. We also allow substitution to vary with smartphone penetration. The results show that telecom-OTT substitutability is strongly market-dependent. In the full-sample IV specification, the implied elasticity is below unity, indicating low substitutability, or gross complementarity, on average across heterogeneous markets. By contrast, the European subsample and GMM robustness specifications imply elasticities above unity, consistent with stronger OTT competitive pressure in digitally mature markets. Smartphone penetration significantly increases the estimated degree of substitution. The findings support a market-specific approach to telecom-OTT convergence and provide evidence relevant to market definition, regulatory asymmetry, net neutrality, and network cost recovery.

title: Rhetoric or Substance? IT Governance, Information Asymmetry, and Innovation in Corporate AI Disclosure: Evidence from Japan

detail.abstract: The newness and rapid adoption of AI technology have increased pressure for corporations to provide AI disclosure. Since AI disclosure is voluntary, this study examines whether the firms' decision to voluntarily disclose AI is related to firms' absorptive capacity of AI adoption measured by their IT governance. Compared to other countries, Japanese firms are more cautious in AI adoption. More importantly, corporate reporting in Japan contains conventional politeness (tatemae) rather than actual intent (honne). Hence, our study examines the role of IT governance and the quality of AI disclosure among Japanese listed firms and the extent to which AI disclosure is related to information asymmetry and firms' innovation. To capture the quality of AI disclosure, we develop three distinct measures that correspond to its readability, rhetoric, and substance. Utilizing textual analysis of 10,085 Japanese firms' annual reports filed through the EDINET during 2021-2024, we find that firms' absorptive capacity of AI technology, measured by IT governance, is positively related to AI disclosure. We also find that more substantive AI disclosure that is congruent with firms' strategy is associated with lower information asymmetry, indicating that investors' absorptive capacity to interpret AI disclosure increases when the disclosure is substantive rather than merely rhetorical. We further find that both the presence of AI disclosure and its substantiveness are positively related to firms' innovation, and that for AI-specific patents, rhetoric and substance relate to innovation in opposite directions, suggesting that firms' rhetorical AI commitments (tatemae) do not always reflect their substantive AI engagement (honne). Heterogeneity analyses indicate that firm size, age, and high technology industries also play varying roles in the relationship between IT governance and AI disclosure, and AI disclosure on information asymmetry and innovation.

title: Structural Determinants of Health Inequity: A Cross-National Efficiency Analysis Using Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) and Tobit Modeling

detail.title: Structural Determinants of Health Inequity: A Cross-National Efficiency Analysis Using Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) and Tobit Modeling

detail.abstract: Despite global commitments to Universal Health Coverage (UHC), structural inequalities in healthcare access persist both within and between nations. Traditional evaluative frameworks often focus linearly on spending benchmarks, failing to capture health system efficiency and the paradox where low out-of-pocket (OOP) metrics in low-income nations can signal absolute barriers to access rather than robust financial protection. This study aims to evaluate cross-national healthcare system efficiency and its structural determinants by analyzing how public resource pooling, out-of-pocket exposure, and physical infrastructure capacity interact with internal domestic income distribution and institutional quality to dictate population health outcomes. Using a cross-sectional, non-parametric frontier efficiency design combined with parametric secondary regression, we compiled national-level data validated for the 2023-2026 global reporting windows across 142 countries utilizing databases from the WHO, the World Bank, and the OECD. Input variables were objectively weighted using the Shannon Entropy Method. Technical efficiency (TE) scores were calculated via an output-oriented Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) under variable returns to scale (VRS) applied to the entropy-scaled inputs. Finally, a two-stage bootstrapped Tobit regression was executed to regress efficiency scores against socioeconomic and environmental covariates. The DEA frontier mapping revealed significant variations in technical efficiency across distinct country income classifications. The second-stage Tobit regression demonstrated that structural income inequality, measured by the Gini Index, significantly suppresses health system efficiency (β =-0.154, p < 0.05), holding input density constant. Conversely, institutional governance quality and public trust exhibited a strong positive relationship with efficiency scores (β = 0.341, p < 0.01), serving as a primary driver of system resilience. Achieving equitable public health outcomes requires moving past static input expansion toward need-based manpower planning and the structural integration of equity into national health financing frameworks. Policy frameworks must integrate redistributive financial mechanisms into health system architectures to mitigate the compounding effects of national income inequality on healthcare efficiency.

title: Representation of Women in Real Estate Funds: Evidence from Switzerland and the UK
affiliations: Lucerne University of Applied Sciences and Arts

detail.title: Representation of Women in Real Estate Funds: Evidence from Switzerland and the UK
detail.abstract:
Here is a draft based on your writing style from the thesis:

This study examines gender representation across Swiss real estate funds and UK real estate investment trusts (REITs), with a focus on boards, executive leadership, asset management, and operational roles. Using publicly available data collected between March and April 2025, 72 Swiss funds and 41 UK REITs were analysed. Gender was identified based on individual names disclosed in fund prospectuses, annual reports, and websites.

The findings show a significant gender imbalance across both markets, with the gap widening at higher levels of seniority. In Swiss funds, women hold 15% of board seats and just 8% of C suite roles. In UK funds, board representation is higher at 39%, but women account for only 20% of executive board members and 15% of board chairs despite holding a majority of non executive positions. No Swiss fund in the sample had a publicly accessible diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policy, compared to approximately 40% of UK funds. No statistically significant relationship was found between the proportion of women on a board and fund performance in either market. Swiss property valuers, an underexplored group, showed similarly low female representation at 19%.

The study contributes to a largely underdeveloped area of research, as Swiss specific analysis of gender representation in real estate funds is almost entirely absent from existing literature. The results point to persistent structural barriers for women, particularly in decision making roles, and highlight the need for greater transparency and intentional action across the sector.

detail.abstract: This study, among many others, provides an initial quantitative contribution to the emerging literature as well as existing empirical evidence regarding contagion risks across cryptocurrency markets over time. Using VAR (Vector Autoregressive) and SVAR (Structural Vector Autoregressive) models with Granger causality, along with Student’s t-copulas, we find that Bitcoin is likely to act as an independent asset in this market, while Ripple and Litecoin tend to be recipients of contagion effects, and Ethereum appears to be a primary source of contagion. Our study offers additional insight into the investigation of contagion risks between both historical and future cryptocurrency values by employing Student’s t-copulas for joint distribution analysis and aims to determine whether these contagion effects remain consistent over time. The results suggest, in both cases, that all cryptocurrencies tend to move negatively in extreme value conditions. Investors are therefore encouraged to pay closer attention to “bad news” and market movement patterns in order to make timely decisions regarding buying, holding, and selling. Note: This thesis reflects the state of cryptocurrency markets and related quantitative models as of 2019-2021. The findings and conclusions are intended to preserve the integrity of the research conducted during this specific time period. I acknowledges that this field evolves rapidly, and an updated analysis may be presented in a forthcoming research paper.

detail.abstract:
This paper argues that Medicare for All Who Want It (M4AWWI) is a politically feasible and economically disciplined public option for the United States. It proposes a voluntary Medicare-based public plan, paired with regulated private supplemental coverage and a federal catastrophic reinsurance backstop, as a middle path between the status quo and immediate single-payer reform. The paper contends that the central failure of the current system is not only uninsurance but a broader “K-shaped” distribution of health outcomes in which income, geography, and insurance status shape morbidity, mortality, and financial insecurity.

The analysis addresses the main objections to a public option, including provider reimbursement, adverse selection, fiscal cost, and political feasibility, and proposes tiered payment adjustments, risk adjustment, and catastrophic reinsurance as stabilizing mechanisms. It further argues that recent Medicaid retrenchment has made a federally anchored fallback plan more urgent, particularly for rural and medically vulnerable populations. Finally, the paper evaluates financing under both orthodox budget frameworks and a Modern Monetary Theory perspective, concluding that the principal barriers to reform are political and institutional rather than economic.

detail.title: Assortative Mating and Education Gradients Within and Across Generations
detail.abstract: We study how assortative mating shapes the composition of education–outcome gradients and how these gradients relate to intergenerational transmission. Using Danish administrative data on family quartets, we decompose own gradients in long-run earnings, disposable income, assets, and wealth into jointly transmitted parental factors, parent-specific transmission, nonparental shared influences, and individual-specific heterogeneity. Earnings and income gradients mainly reflect jointly transmitted parental factors and individual-specific heterogeneity; assets and especially wealth mainly reflect parent-specific transmission. Comparing families facing different parental access to middle schools, we show that the composition of financial gradients varies by educational opportunity, while labor market gradients are largely invariant.

title: The Global Debt Trap: Structural Dependence and Credit Expansion in the Modern Economic System

detail.title: The Global Debt Trap: Structural Dependence and Credit Expansion in the Modern Economic System

detail.abstract: Global debt has become one of the defining characteristics of the modern economic system. Over recent decades, governments, businesses, financial institutions, and households have accumulated unprecedented levels of debt, while successive economic crises have been addressed through further credit expansion, increased liquidity, and monetary intervention. This essay examines whether the continuous growth of global debt constitutes merely a policy challenge or a structural feature of the contemporary economic framework. It argues that the relationship between economic growth and credit expansion has evolved from a temporary stabilisation mechanism into a fundamental dependence of the system itself. While economic growth remains uncertain and depends on multiple factors, debt accumulation follows a more predictable and persistent trajectory, creating an increasing asymmetry between future obligations and the productive capacity required to service them. Drawing upon recent international data, the essay highlights that the highest debt levels are frequently found among the world's most advanced economies. This observation suggests that the expansion of debt is not simply the result of poor management but may be linked to the structure of the financial system itself. The essay concludes by posing the question of whether long-term economic stability can continue to rely on the ongoing expansion of borrowing and argues that the discussion should shift from debt management toward an examination of the deeper mechanisms that drive its persistent accumulation.

title: How Do Beliefs About Future Events Affect Asset Prices? Evidence From Prediction Markets
affiliations: and

detail.title: How Do Beliefs About Future Events Affect Asset Prices? Evidence From Prediction Markets
detail.abstract: How beliefs about future events-and the disagreement among them-shape asset prices is a central question in finance, but existing empirical measures of investor beliefs are indirect, low-frequency, or aggregated. We address this using the universe of transactionlevel data from Polymarket, a money-backed prediction market, over June 2024 through March 2026. From the same transaction tape, in the common metric of probabilities, we construct two high-frequency primitives: a price-entropy measure of consensus uncertainty and a dollar-volume-weighted measure of investor disagreement. We establish three results. First, the prediction market and the U.S. equity market are informationally integrated in both directions: stocks lead Polymarket within the trading day, while overnight Polymarket innovations predict the next morning's equity open. Second, disagreement positively predicts next-day stock returns, consistent with compensation for unspanned macro state risk rather than mispricing. Third, consensus uncertainty predicts lower near-term equity volume and realised volatility, with the volatility released as uncertainty resolves, so it governs the timing of repricing rather than its level. A parsimonious heterogeneous-beliefs model rationalises the full pattern: disagreement is priced, while uncertainty is traded.

title: The Future of Investor-State Dispute Settlement: Balancing Sovereignty and Foreign Investment in Developing Economies

detail.title: The Future of Investor-State Dispute Settlement: Balancing Sovereignty and Foreign Investment in Developing Economies
detail.abstract: Investor-State Dispute Settlement (ISDS) mechanisms remain controversial as they attempt to balance investor protection with host-state sovereignty. Developing economies, particularly in Africa, often face criticism that ISDS undermines their ability to regulate in the public interest while still being essential to attract foreign direct investment (FDI). This paper analyzes the historical evolution of ISDS, the legitimacy crisis it faces, and reform initiatives such as the UNCITRAL Working Group III proposals. Using Nigeria and other African economies as case studies, it evaluates how reforms can create a more equitable system that upholds sovereign regulatory power while ensuring investor confidence. The paper recommends a calibrated package of substantive treaty language, procedural safeguards, investor obligations, capacitybuilding, and phased implementation strategies to reconcile sovereignty and investment promotion in developing contexts. By situating these reforms within broader international investment law discourse, the paper outlines practical pathways for policymakers to craft a forward-looking ISDS framework that sustains development goals and legal certainty.

detail.abstract: This paper identifies and characterizes a structural property, hitherto unnoted, in a class of growth models: when a firm's accumulating factor (capital or a knowledge base) may grow without bound, but its value output enters profit only through a bounded saturating map, firm value is finite for every positive discount rate and is independent of the growth rate of accumulation. We call this property saturation decoupling. The main theorem delivers three conclusions: (i) value is unconditionally finite, , even when the state diverges and even at the AK knife-edge or super-exponential growth; (ii) (long-run average profit); (iii) (initial profit). The latter two are the economic incarnations of the final- and initialvalue theorems of the Laplace transform, and they furnish a falsifiable characterization that is exactly opposite to standard AK endogenous growth: in AK, diverges as ; here it converges to long-run average profit. We show how the mechanism arises from a concrete coverage-based growth dynamics, and discuss its implications for valuing high-accumulation, low-current-cash-flow firms.

affiliations: Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU) and Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU)

detail.title: On the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations: Longevity, Institutions, and Patience
detail.abstract: We reconsider some of the central aspects in Adam Smith's work in light of advances in research on long-run development. The main argument is that future orientation - "patience" - represents a key unifying feature in the mechanisms of long-run development. This feature appears to have been part of Smith's argument in various manifestations. We develop the argument along the lines of a simple conceptual framework and discuss the consequences of the influence of life expectancy and institutional quality on the patience embodied in the population for the emergence of development traps. We then illustrate how a feedback from patience to improved life expectancy and institutions can initiate a process of sustained development.

title: Three Stage DG–ESS Planning Using Tianji’s Horse Racing Optimization for Hosting Capacity Enhancement in Radial Distribution Networks
affiliations: Al-Azhar University, Al-Azhar University and Faculty of Engineering (grails), Al-Azhar University, Cairo, Egypt

detail.title: Three Stage DG–ESS Planning Using Tianji’s Horse Racing Optimization for Hosting Capacity Enhancement in Radial Distribution Networks
detail.abstract: Distributed generation based on renewable energy sources is expanding rapidly in African and global distribution networks. Still, its hosting capacity is often constrained by voltage violations, thermal overloads, and increased technical losses. This paper proposes a three stage planning framework that reinforces radial distribution grids by coordinating distributed generation (DG) and battery energy storage systems (ESS) while preserving secure operation. In Stage 1, a multi-objective optimization problem is formulated to maximize DG hosting capacity and minimize active power losses, subject to voltage magnitude, thermal, and DG penetration constraints; Tianji’s Horse Racing Optimization (THRO) and benchmark metaheuristics are employed to determine optimal DG locations and sizes. In Stage 2, the selected DG configuration is evaluated under a 24 hour load profile, and a dynamic loss sensitivity factor (LSF) index is developed by aggregating hourly LSF values to rank candidate buses for ESS placement. In Stage 3, ESS units are optimally sized and scheduled in charge/idle/discharge modes to transfer Energy from off-peak to peak hours, subject to state-of-charge and power limits, thereby reducing daily losses without altering the DG hosting capacity definition. The framework is validated on the IEEE 33 bus radial distribution system and a real 59 bus Egyptian network. Results show that THRO provides superior DG siting and sizing compared with recent metaheuristics and that dynamic LSF based ESS integration yields additional loss reduction and annual loss cost savings, demonstrating the effectiveness of coordinated DG–ESS planning for emerging distribution systems.

title: The Neglected Encouragement Effect in Small-Scale Research Tournaments
affiliations: ,  and Duke University - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Neglected Encouragement Effect in Small-Scale Research Tournaments
detail.abstract: Competition in research tournaments has two facets. More rivals dilute the expected prize, but they also make any current discovery less safe and thereby increase the value of continued search. We study this tradeoff in a continuous-time Poisson version of Taylor's 1995 model, in which contestants search sequentially, stop when their best draw exceeds an equilibrium threshold, and compete for a fixed prize. The equilibrium threshold reflects both prize dilution and the previously overlooked countervailing encouragement effect. We show that the encouragement effect can dominate in small or short contests, while prize dilution dominates once contests become sufficiently large or long. Thus equilibrium effort is single-peaked in the number of contestants: competition can stimulate innovation before it discourages it.

title: Beyond the Target: U.S. Sanctions, Inventor Mobility, and the Unintended Knowledge Diffusion
affiliations: Shenzhen University, Peking University, Peking University - Guanghua School of Management, Department of Applied Economics and INSE at Peking University

detail.title: Beyond the Target: U.S. Sanctions, Inventor Mobility, and the Unintended Knowledge Diffusion
detail.abstract: Targeted technology controls aim to constrain sanctioned firms, but may diffuse inventive capacity beyond them. We study this unintended consequence through Chinese firms' additions to the U.S. Entity List, using a universal inventor-firm panel from Chinese patents, 2014-2022. Tracking inventors across employers, we find that listing raises departures by 8.1 percentage points without reducing movers' patenting. Exit is strongest at firms reliant on U.S. inputs and with thinner knowledge bases. Recipient firms learn from movers' source firms' revealed comparative advantage, redirect innovation, stimulate incumbent patenting, and intensify innovation-market competition. These spillovers offset over one quarter of sanctioned firms' innovation losses.

title: Role of Freshwater Turtles in River Ecosystem Cleaning With Focus on Tamil Nadu, India
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Role of Freshwater Turtles in River Ecosystem Cleaning With Focus on Tamil Nadu, India
detail.abstract: Freshwater turtles, particularly softshell species, perform a critical but underappreciated ecological function: biological self-purification of river systems. This article examines the three primary mechanisms through which turtles contribute to water quality scavenging organic waste, nutrient cycling, and algae control drawing on experimental evidence from peer-reviewed literature, with a specific focus on Tamil Nadu's major river systems (Cauvery, Thamirabarani, Vaigai, and Bhavani). Field data from the Cauvery River document severe exceedances of BOD, COD, and TDS relative to permissible limits, precisely the conditions where turtle populations historically provided ecological regulation. The recent re-documentation of Leith's Softshell Turtle (Nilssonia leithii) in the Kaveri delta after 30 years is analysed as an indicator of partial ecological recovery. The article also reviews government conservation initiatives including the Cauvery South Wildlife Sanctuary and the Namami Gange programme's turtle reintroduction efforts. The findings support the case for integrating freshwater turtle conservation into river restoration policy frameworks in India.
