detail.abstract: We formalize NRFS, a sequence generator in which the generating grammar the operators and functions of the expression itself is a recursively randomized variable rather than a xed function, and whose output is ltered through a gate of statistical tests. We model the construction as an environment-randomized branching process whose candidate law E k is enriched at each rejection, and we study the conditioned output together with its detectability. Three results are established. First, the gate guarantees termination if and only if the acceptance probability is uniformly bounded below; self-perturbation alone does not (Theorem 1). Second, the conditioned output admits a collision bound P[S = S ′ ] ≤ 2-H∞(S) , which is the precise form of the system's non-reproducibility claim, and which is capped by the entropy of the implementation's randomness source (Theorem 2). Third the central result we prove that a nite battery gate is self-defeating against a baseline-aware adversary: the membership indicator D A (s) = 1[s ∈ A] is itself an ecient distinguisher of advantage 1-α, where α is the probability the reference (honest) distribution assigns to the acceptance region. Consequently, indistinguishability with respect to a nite family of tests does not transfer to indistinguishability against an adversary that models the baseline trac; conditioning the output to pass a battery makes it anomalously clean, and too clean is the signature (Theorem 3). We give the nite, applied analogue of the Martin-Löf characterization (no nite battery captures randomness), reframe the digital-asset privacy application as resistance against a declared family rather than unconditional anonymity, and state the open problems including the baseline-matching tradeo and the absence of any hardness assumption, which removes the basis for security claims against quantum or unbounded adversaries.

title: The Market Abuse Regulation and the Use of General Clauses Thereunder

detail.title: The Market Abuse Regulation and the Use of General Clauses Thereunder
detail.abstract: The EU Market Abuse Regulation ("MAR") provides, in the context of EU financial markets law, a striking example of the importance that so-called general clauses can have within a given regulatory regime. The text of the MAR-notoriously structured along two main regulatory veins concerning, on the one hand, inside information, and, on the other hand, market manipulation-is marked by the presence of a number of legal provisions with broad scopes, which are not expressly defined. Such provisions are typical of the complex and articulated universe of general clauses, whose notions and concepts are underpinned by a considerable interpretative elasticity. As a consequence, the understanding of the legal content embedded in such provisions necessarily relies on external criteria. The paper aims at providing a framework for the interpretation of such provisions, by linking them to the ECMH.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Its Impact on Human Interaction and Society
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and Its Impact on Human Interaction and Society
detail.abstract: This paper explores the growing role of artificial intelligence in modern society, focusing on its impact across transportation, healthcare, education, media, and the economy. It highlights how AI is transforming everyday life by improving efficiency, decision-making, and innovation. At the same time, the paper also examines challenges such as job displacement and ethical concerns. By analyzing both the benefits and limitations, this study aims to present a balanced understanding of how AI is shaping the future and its influence on human interaction and society.

title: Machine Learning Analysis of Public Willingness to Pay for Kelp Forest Restoration in Norway
affiliations: and University of Galway

detail.title: Machine Learning Analysis of Public Willingness to Pay for Kelp Forest Restoration in Norway
detail.abstract: This study applies machine learning (ML) classification methods to a discrete choice experiment dataset on public preferences for kelp forest restoration in Norway. While a random parameter logit (RPL) model estimates marginal willingness to pay for ecological attributes, the ML framework addresses three questions the parametric model cannot: how well observable characteristics predict the binary decision to support restoration; whether cost sensitivity follows the linear pattern assumed by the price coefficient; and how predicted support is distributed across the population. Using logistic regression, the random forest ML approach and gradient boosting, the analysis shows moderate out-of-sample discrimination. Socio-demographic characteristics, particularly age, marine recreational activity, tertiary education, and environmental organisation membership, are key predictors of heterogeneity in restoration support decisions, followed by ecological design attributes. This indicates that respondent identity matters when predicting whether a policy option is supported at all in a choice experiment situation. The ML models also reveal nonlinear cost sensitivity not captured by the linear price coefficient. Predicted support is stable between €5 and €20 per year but declines sharply beyond €30, indicating a cost range for public financing decisions. The empirical distribution of predicted support is strongly left-skewed, and decile lift analysis confirms that low-support segments can be identified for targeted engagement. These findings show how ML methods complement existing econometric approaches in environmental economics, providing insights for restoration programmes, cost threshold identification, and stakeholder communication strategies.

title: Specialization, Structural Change, and Cluster Policy in Berlin: A Location-Quotient and Shift-Share Analysis

detail.title: Specialization, Structural Change, and Cluster Policy in Berlin: A Location-Quotient and Shift-Share Analysis
detail.abstract: Berlin presents a paradox: a capital city-state with values higher than national average for output and productivity, yet carries one of Germany's highest unemployment rates and a wide distributional gap. This paper characterizes the structure, performance, and policy alignment of the Berlin economy using official social-insurance employment data for 2019 to 2025, combining location quotients, a full three-way shift-share decomposition, a structured SWOT assessment, an evaluation of the innoBB cluster strategy and the institutions that deliver it, and an appraisal against the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. The location quotient identifies a service economy concentrated in knowledge-intensive and creative activities, led by information and communication at 2.21, which together form the region's export base. Employment grew by 10.2 percent over the period, more than double the national rate of 4.4 percent, and the shift-share shows that the competitive component of that growth, near 53,000 jobs, exceeds the industry-mix component of about 34,500, evidence that Berlin's expansion reflects genuine local competitiveness rather than a merely favourable sector composition. The diversified structure, indicated by a low concentration of employment across sectors, is consistent with the region's comparatively mild contraction in 2020. The innoBB strategy corresponds closely to the measured specialization and advances the goals of innovation, clean energy, health, and partnership, but it is silent on decent work, poverty, inequality, and gender, the same distributional weaknesses that the SWOT and the institutional assessment independently identify alongside an unemployment rate near 10.5 percent against a national 6.4 percent. The central task for a successor strategy, the analysis concludes, is not to add clusters but to connect the city's innovative core to its excluded labour market.

title: Reshaping Urban Space: Evidence of a TOD Policy in Curitiba, Brazil
affiliations: and Federal University of Parana

detail.title: Reshaping Urban Space: Evidence of a TOD Policy in Curitiba, Brazil
detail.abstract: Transit-oriented development has become a key strategy for promoting compact, accessible, and sustainable urban growth, but there is still limited causal evidence of its effectiveness in reshaping urban spatial structures, especially in middle-income cities. This study examines the Green Line project in Curitiba, Brazil, a large-scale TOD initiative that combined Bus Rapid Transit investments with zoning reforms to encourage higher-density, mixed-use development along a former highway corridor. Using variation in implementation timing across the BRT corridor, we apply quasi-experimental difference-indifferences and event-study models to high-resolution longitudinal data on population, housing, firms, and employment to estimate the policy's impacts. The results show significant but uneven urban changes: population density along the treated corridor increased by about 11%, with stronger effects in areas where BRT infrastructure was introduced earlier. Residential verticalization was mainly observed in fully operational segments. Conversely, there is little evidence that the intervention significantly boosted local economic activity in retail and services. These findings demonstrate that TOD policies can quickly influence residential location choices through improved access and flexible land-use regulations, but broader economic shifts tend to occur more gradually and depend on infrastructure completion.

title: Waste Collection Efficiency Drivers Beyond Scale: When Size Matters and When It Does Not
affiliations: University of Florence, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Florence and University of Florence - Department of Economics and Management

detail.title: Waste Collection Efficiency Drivers Beyond Scale: When Size Matters and When It Does Not
detail.abstract: The relationship between scale and efficiency in municipal waste management remains unsettled, with mixed evidence on the existence and sources of economies of scale. Empirical studies predominantly assess performance at the municipal level, despite waste services increasingly being delivered by providers operating across multiple municipalities. This may confound scale effects with the underlying organization of service provision. Using a novel provider-level dataset covering the Italian municipal waste collection sector, this paper estimates eco-efficiency through a robust non-parametric order-m frontier. Our results show that size matters for efficiency only when conditioned on the fragmentation of service provision. Rather than scale, the structure of service provision emerges as a key dimension in explaining performance. Providers operating within a single municipality exhibit the lowest eco-efficiency levels, suggesting that limited territorial scope constrains performance. By contrast, eco-efficiency improves when activity extends across multiple municipalities, and waste generation is more uniformly distributed across the service area, linking more balanced collection patterns to stronger outcomes. Vertical integration also shows a positive relationship with eco-efficiency, suggesting that coordination across multiple stages of the waste management chain may strengthen collection and transport activities.

title: Learning to Vaccinate: Bounded-rational Decisions, Networked Contagion, and Social Dilemmas in a Spatiotemporal Epidemic Model
affiliations: Cleveland State University - Economics and Fordham University

detail.title: Learning to Vaccinate: Bounded-rational Decisions, Networked Contagion, and Social Dilemmas in a Spatiotemporal Epidemic Model
detail.abstract: We present an agent-based computational model of vaccination in which individuals adapt their probabilistic choices through Experience-Weighted Attraction (EWA) learning as they update perceptions of infection risk over time. Embedded within a seasonal epidemic framework, the model examines long-term vaccination behavior among individuals connected through limited-size interpersonal contact networks. We compare steady-state vaccination outcomes with socially optimal levels, identifying zones of social dilemma characterized by both under- and over-vaccination. Our analysis isolates the roles of (1) learning dynamics and (2) network structure in shaping contagion and vaccination. We further incorporate spatial heterogeneity by partitioning the population into non-overlapping regions with cross-regional contacts, allowing us to examine how regional disparities and inter-regional connectivity shape vaccination behavior, infection risk, and overall epidemic size, as well as the policy implications of social distancing mandates on vaccine uptake. Simulation results show that greater belief-based updating raises steady-state vaccination coverage, while social distancing—modeled as a reduction in network size—inadvertently depresses vaccination incentives, partially offsetting its direct epidemiological benefits. The social dilemma shifts from under- to over-vaccination as networks shrink or regional isolation strengthens, and stronger regionalization amplifies cross-regional disparities in both vaccination uptake and infection exposure.

detail.abstract: On October 19, 1976, the Copyright Act of 1976 will celebrate its fiftieth anniversary. Published as part of a commemorative special issue on the internationalization of U.S. copyright law, this article examines the cross-jurisdictional influence, or “Washington effect,” of the U.S. Copyright Act, including both the 1976 Copyright Act and subsequent legislative enactments. It begins by examining the United States’s transformation from a country offering limited protection to nonresident foreign authors to one championing high levels of copyright protection around the world. The article then provides two leading illustrations of U.S. copyright law transplants—namely, fair use and the notice-and-takedown procedure. It concludes by drawing five key takeaways from the process of transplanting U.S. copyright standards around the world. The discussion reveals the extent and limitations of the Washington effect, or cross-jurisdictional influence, of the U.S. Copyright Act.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education: Transforming Teaching, Learning, and Academic Assessment
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education: Transforming Teaching, Learning, and Academic Assessment
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in higher education, redefining traditional approaches to teaching, learning, and academic assessment. Universities across the world are increasingly integrating AI-driven technologies to enhance educational effectiveness, personalize learning experiences, optimize administrative efficiency, and improve institutional decision-making. This study examines the growing influence of artificial intelligence in higher education and evaluates its role in transforming pedagogical practices, student engagement, and assessment mechanisms. Using a narrative review methodology, the article synthesizes evidence from scholarly literature on AI applications in university settings, focusing on adaptive learning systems, intelligent tutoring technologies, predictive analytics, automated grading systems, and generative AI tools. The study highlights how AI contributes to individualized learning pathways, facilitates real-time feedback, enhances student retention strategies, and supports data-informed instructional decisions. At the same time, concerns regarding academic integrity, algorithmic bias, ethical governance, privacy, technological inequality, and overdependence on automated systems are critically examined. Findings indicate that while AI significantly improves educational accessibility, efficiency, and personalization, successful implementation requires institutional readiness, faculty digital competence, transparent governance structures, and ethical policy frameworks. Furthermore, universities must adopt balanced approaches that integrate human pedagogical judgment with intelligent technologies to maintain educational quality and academic credibility. The study concludes that artificial intelligence represents not merely a technological innovation but a structural transformation in higher education, with the potential to redefine the future of teaching, learning, and academic evaluation if implemented responsibly and inclusively.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a novel options pricing framework that explicitly incorporates climate transition risk as a time-varying, regime-dependent jump component within a stochastic volatility model. While existing literature has examined physical climate risk and financial asset pricing separately, no study has yet modeled the interaction between climate policy shocks, volatility regimes, and the implied volatility surface in a unified options-pricing framework. . Using a dataset of 21 years of daily options data on the S&P 500, energy sector ETFs (XLE), and ESG-screened equity indices across 12 markets (2005–2026), we estimate the model via Efficient Method of Moments (EMM) and document three principal findings. First, climate jump intensity significantly contributes to the implied volatility smirk, explaining up to 18% of the at-the-money implied volatility spread between carbon-intensive and ESG indices. Second, the climate risk premium embedded in out-of-the-money put options on fossil fuel firms has increased by 340 basis points since the Paris Agreement (2015), while OTM calls on clean energy have seen a 220 bps premium compression. Third, standard Black-Scholes and Heston models produce systematic mispricing of 5.2–11.7% for options on carbon-intensive underlyings, corrected by our Climate-Adjusted Heston (CAH) model.

title:
The Readable Cosmos:
Science, Consciousness, and the Qurʼanic Concept of Āyāt
affiliations: Independent

detail.title:
The Readable Cosmos:
Science, Consciousness, and the Qurʼanic Concept of Āyāt
detail.abstract:
This study examines the relationship between scientific inquiry,
consciousness, and the Qurʾānic concept of āyāt (signs). It argues
that the perceived conflict between science and religion often
stems not from science itself but from scientism—the extension of
scientific methodology into a comprehensive metaphysical
worldview. The study first distinguishes methodological science
from scientism and explores the implications of this distinction for
the science–religion debate. It then analyzes the Qurʾānic concept
of āyāt, arguing that the Qurʾān presents the cosmos as ordered,
intelligible, and open to rational investigation. Finally, the paper
engages contemporary debates on consciousness, mathematics,
and the limits of reductionism. Drawing on analytic philosophy,
philosophy of mind, philosophy of religion, and classical Islamic
thought, it proposes that the Qurʾānic notion of āyāt provides a
framework in which cosmic intelligibility and conscious subjectivity
are philosophically interconnected rather than accidental. The study
neither treats scientific gaps as proof of theism nor claims that the
Qurʾān contains hidden scientific predictions, but argues that the
exclusion of metaphysical reflection remains philosophically
contested.

title: Diagnosing and Mitigating Artifact-Induced Shortcut Learning in Histopathology Image Classification
affiliations: Taiyuan University of Technology, Taiyuan University of Technology, Taiyuan University of Technology, Taiyuan University of Technology and Taiyuan University of Technology

detail.title: Diagnosing and Mitigating Artifact-Induced Shortcut Learning in Histopathology Image Classification
detail.abstract: Deep learning classifiers for histopathological image classification often degrade across institutions. A key mechanism is artifact-induced shortcut learning, where classifiers exploit artifact-related cues statistically associated with diagnostic labels rather than tissue morphology. Such bias is hard to detect because performance may remain high when the artifact-label correlation is preserved, yet deteriorate when this correlation shifts. Moreover, since the bias is encoded in learned representations, input-level correction alone is insufficient.We propose Artifact-Invariant Representation Learning (AIRL), a training-time debiasing framework that uses Controlled Local Artifact Restoration (CLAR) as an internal view-construction module. CLAR constructs multi-severity artifact views and provides soft artifact masks; the debiasing module performs feature-space alignment via cross-severity cosine consistency, a mask-guided suppression gate, and a stop-gradient auxiliary artifact-perception head. In this study, CLAR is instantiated with oracle restoration and masks from the synthetic contamination protocol, isolating the representation-level debiasing effect under exactly known conditions. Experiments on NCT-CRC-HE-100K and frozenfeature diagnostics on the external HistoArtifacts dataset demonstrate that AIRL substantially reduces artifact dependence (balanced accuracy 0.698 → 0.947, feature drift -4.1×, probing accuracy 0.953 → 0.762) while preserving classification performance (AUC 0.999), outperforming five shortcut-mitigation baselines, and showing partial transfer to real spatially localized artifacts. Validation on real multi-site whole-slide cohorts is needed for clinical conclusions.

detail.abstract: Investor sentiment serves as a pivotal driver of price dynamics, yet its precise measurement faces challenges stemming from data heterogeneity and nonlinear transmission mechanisms. This study systematically reviews existing methods for investor sentiment measurement and dissect limitations of current approaches. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework for measuring investor sentiment by integrating both subjective and objective data based on fuzzy logic theory. The principal component analysis technique is employed to reduce the dimensionality of daily market behavior data and extract representative sentiment components; the threshold parameters within the fuzzy logic module are dynamically calibrated using subjective survey data, and asymmetric membership functions are introduced to capture the threshold effects in emotional transmission. With these techniques, we develop two new sentiment indicators. Empirical analyses demonstrate that the proposed indices significantly outperform traditional indicators in short-term forecasting, providing a robust and sensitive tool for real-time risk monitoring and investment strategy optimization. Furthermore, the methodological framework is designed for cross-market adaptability, as localized data can be substituted to extend its application to European and other international equity markets, thereby providing a versatile instrument for behavioral finance research and cross-border portfolio management.

detail.abstract: Regional inequality policy typically asks one question: where is the gap largest? This paper argues that this question, while necessary, is insufficient. Drawing on firm-level sigma convergence analysis covering 22.85 million observations across 81 Turkish provinces (2006-2024), we show that the geography of current inequality and the geography of inequality trends are systematically different. The Borluk Stratification Index (BSI) decomposes inequality into a Level component and a Trend component, enabling simultaneous targeting of both dimensions. Provinces that reduce current inequality are concentrated in large western urban centers; provinces that improve the inequality trajectory are distributed across Anatolia. No single province functions as a national locomotive. These findings suggest that effective regional policy requires dual targeting: addressing the stock of inequality and the flow of inequality change are distinct tasks that point to different geographies.

title: Borluk Stratification Index (BSI): A Layered Approach to Firm-Level Inequality Measurement

detail.title: Borluk Stratification Index (BSI): A Layered Approach to Firm-Level Inequality Measurement

detail.abstract: Existing inequality measures, including the widely used Gini coefficient, share a common structural limitation: they treat firm distributions as homogeneous and rely on mean-based statistics that are highly sensitive to extreme values. This working paper introduces the Borluk Stratification Index (BSI), a two-component inequality measure designed specifically for firm-level data. The Level component applies a median absolute deviation (MAD/median) approach across four firm-size layers-micro, small, medium, and large-with differentiated weights that reflect the policy relevance of each layer. The Trend component converts the annual Level series into a directional score (0-100) using exponentially weighted averages that prioritize recent observations. Both components are calibrated on theoretical rather than empirical bounds, enabling cross-time and crosscountry comparability. Applied to 22.85 million firm-year observations from Turkey (2006-2024), BSI yields a Level score of 1.64 and a Trend score of 62, indicating moderate inequality with a mild improvement tendency. The index is fully reproducible and openly documented.

title: Beyond Performance: Replacing a Human Coworker with AI Enhances Motivation
affiliations: EM Lyon (Ecole de Management de Lyon),  and

detail.title: Beyond Performance: Replacing a Human Coworker with AI Enhances Motivation
detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly reshaping the workplace, yet its long-term impact depends not only on productivity gains but also on its effects on human motivation. Prior research has documented performance improvements when humans are augmented with AI, but little is known about the motivational consequences of replacing a human coworker with GenAI. Drawing on self-determination theory and team climate theory, we develop and test a framework predicting how GenAI affects individual motivation. In a preregistered experiment (n = 1,091), participants completed a creative task either with another human or with GenAI under identical conditions. Consistent with recent evidence, human-AI teams outperformed all-human teams (Cohen's d = 0.3). Contrary to concerns that automation could erode intrinsic motivation, collaborating with GenAI increased perceived relatedness, competence, autonomy, job satisfaction, and interest (Cohen's d = 0.2-0.5). These findings suggest that the psychological mechanisms underlying cooperation are sufficiently flexible to extend to automated partners, with important implications for work design.

title: Tariff Shocks as Natural Experiments: Pass-Through, Market Structure, and Antitrust Risk
affiliations: Berkeley Research Group, LLC

detail.title: Tariff Shocks as Natural Experiments: Pass-Through, Market Structure, and Antitrust Risk
detail.abstract: Tariffs commonly are discussed as instruments of trade policy in macroeconomics or industrial strategy to support specific domestic industries. However, tariffs are more analytically revealing from a competition-policy perspective, as they are usually large, policy-driven common cost shocks imposed simultaneously on competing firms that can affect products within a market. This feature makes tariff episodes valuable for antitrust analysis. When costs rise for many rival firms at once, pricing can move in parallel even in fully competitive markets. At the same time, similar cost pressures can make coordination more attractive and easier to sustain. Tariff episodes then create an environment in which both tacit and coordinated explanations for price increases simultaneously become plausible.

title: Firm-Level Regional Inequality in Turkey: A Sigma Convergence Analysis, 2006-2024

detail.abstract: This paper examines regional inequality dynamics in Turkey over the 2006-2024 period using firmlevel administrative data from the Entrepreneur Information System (GBS). Drawing on 22.85 million firm-year observations across 81 provinces and 19 years, we apply sigma convergence analysis at three spatial scales: provincial (81 NUTS-3 units), regional (26 NUTS-2 units), and within-region (firm-level dispersion inside each region). Net sales and gross value added are deflated using producer price indices (base year 2006). The findings reveal a three-phase pattern: convergence during 2006-2012 (-20.8% net sales,-9.5% gross value added), near-stagnation during 2013-2019, and sharp divergence after 2020 (+32.6% net sales, +25.4% gross value added). Crisis-exclusion tests confirm that some convergence episodes partially reflect deterioration rather than genuine catch-up. Withinregion analysis identifies club convergence: firms converge inside all 26 NUTS-2 regions for net sales, yet between-region dispersion widened by 38% over the full period. No locomotive province is identified at the national level. The results suggest polarization rather than systemic convergence.

title: Equilibrium World Models
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley and University of Lausanne - School of Economics and Business Administration (HEC-Lausanne)

detail.title: Equilibrium World Models
detail.abstract: We introduce Equilibrium World Models (EWMs), a deep-learning method for globally solving dynamic stochastic models that feature rare disasters, binding constraints, and counterfactual states. Standard unsupervised neural-network-based solvers impose equilibrium conditions only on states generated by their own simulated policy. Their solutions can therefore be selfconfirming: accurate on the simulated path, but untested off it, sensitive to initialization, and costly when expectations must be recomputed at each step. EWMs change the computational representation, not the economics. They enforce the model's exact equilibrium conditions on a broader, model-generated distribution of ordinary, rare, stressed, and counterfactual states. They carry the continuation with a learned surrogate, but certify the resulting policy strictly against the true equilibrium conditions. We provide an error decomposition, an off-path residual bound, and a convergence result linking self-confirming solutions to rational-expectations equilibria. We demonstrate EWMs through a sequence of test cases that isolate the main pathologies of classical deep-learning solvers and then scale them to richer economies. In a rare-disaster Brock-Mirman laboratory, coverage reduces disaster-region residuals by an order of magnitude. In a rare-disaster Brock–Mirman laboratory, coverage reduces disaster-region residuals by an order of magnitude. In a high-dimensional international real-business-cycle model, classical deep-learning solvers fail from all random starts, whereas EWMs converge from nearly all and evaluate continuations up to two orders of magnitude less often. When actions move transition measures, EWMs use action-conditioned continuations to recover the relevant policy margin. In a heterogeneous-agent economy with aggregate risk, EWMs compress the numerical representation of the wealth distribution by at least 25× while imposing exact full-distribution rational-expectations conditions.

title: Many Suppliers Win, Few Capture the Value: Participation and Value Concentration in EU Public Procurement

detail.title: Many Suppliers Win, Few Capture the Value: Participation and Value Concentration in EU Public Procurement

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available administrative data and does not require ethical approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Public procurement markets often appear competitive based on the number of participating suppliers. However, participation-based indicators may mask substantial concentration in the allocation of economic value, a gap that participation-based monitoring is not designed to detect.

This paper introduces Value–Count Divergence (VCD), a diagnostic measure that quantifies the mismatch between supplier rankings by contract count and by contract value. Using award data from Tenders Electronic Daily (TED) across 19 EU procurement domains (2018–2022), we show that VCD is pervasive and heterogeneous: in a typical domain, a supplier’s rank by contract count is only weakly correlated with its rank by value. Markets that appear broadly accessible in terms of participation are often dominated by a small number of suppliers in terms of spending.

To investigate the structural sources of value concentration, we develop a classification framework identifying suppliers that capture the top decile of procurement value in a subsequent period, under a strict temporal split design. Value captors are highly predictable (mean AUC ≈ 0.91), and a model relying solely on network-structural features performs nearly as well as a full model including value-history variables (ΔAUC ≈ 0.01), indicating that structural position within the procurement network—rather than accumulated financial advantage—is the primary driver of value concentration.

These findings reveal a systematic misalignment between regulatory signals and economic outcomes. We propose that procurement oversight be complemented with distributional and network-based indicators alongside conventional participation measures. VCD is directly computable from existing procurement data and can be readily integrated into oversight systems as an early-warning diagnostic of emerging value concentration.

detail.title: Heterogeneous Spatio-temporal Effects of the Screwworm-induced Border Closure on US Cattle Basis Prices
detail.abstract: The U.S. suspended imports of live cattle from Mexico beginning in 2024 following the detection of New World Screwworm (NWS) in Mexico. This measure was an effort to prevent an outbreak of NWS into the U.S., which could cause significant economic losses. Mexican cattle are an important source of feeder cattle supplies for the U.S., and closing the border represents a major supply shock. We quantify the impacts of closing the border on domestic cattle markets. We find that feeder cattle basis strengthened following the closure. The magnitude of this effect depends on a market's proximity to the border and the duration of the closure.

title: Survival Analysis Approach for Predicting Educational Plan Policyholder Surrendering The Policy: A case study of Banc-assurance of a known bank in Ghana

detail.title: Survival Analysis Approach for Predicting Educational Plan Policyholder Surrendering The Policy: A case study of Banc-assurance of a known bank in Ghana
detail.abstract: Educational plan insurance policies serve as critical financial instruments combining savings and protection functions to secure funding for children's education. Despite their intended benefits, increasing surrender rates threaten both beneficiary welfare and insurer sustainability. This study examines the timing and determinants of policy surrender among Educational Plan policyholders in a bancassurance setting using survival analysis techniques, drawing on secondary data from a Ghanaian financial institution spanning 2016 to 2021. The Kaplan-Meier estimator is employed to characterize policyholder retention patterns and estimate survival probabilities over time, while the Cox proportional hazards model quantifies the independent effects of age and gender on the hazard of surrender. Diagnostic testing via Schoenfeld residuals revealed a violation of the proportional hazards assumption for age, necessitating a stratified Cox model with gender as the stratification variable. Restricted mean survival time (RMST) analysis provides a complementary, assumption-free measure of policy persistence across demographic subgroups. Findings indicate that surrender risk is heavily concentrated in the first 36 months of policy tenure, with a median survival time of approximately 12 months. Age emerges as the dominant predictor of surrender behavior, with each additional year associated with a 1.9% reduction in surrender hazard, while male policyholders exhibit a 6.1% higher hazard than their female counterparts. RMST analysis reveals that policyholders aged 50 years and above remain on their policies approximately 7.5 months longer than those under 30 years. Substantial branch-level heterogeneity is also documented, with early surrender rates ranging from 71.7% to 95.7%, though negligible temporal persistence in branch risk (r =-0.066, p = 0.687) suggests that poor branch performance is not structurally entrenched. A key limitation of the study is that the dataset comprises exclusively surrendered policies; policyholders who retained coverage throughout the observation period are unobserved. All survival estimates are therefore conditional on eventual surrender and should not be interpreted as population-level retention probabilities. This constraint reflects data availability rather than methodological choice and is addressed transparently throughout the analysis.

detail.abstract: When contract law invokes a reasonableness standard, whose standard applies-and what kind? Doctrine prescribes external benchmarks-industry custom, community expectations-rather than individual moral judgment. Two pre-registered experiments (N = 2,342) test which benchmark laypeople apply across twenty-five contractual scenarios. Personal injunctive norms-what individuals believe one ought to do-most closely track reasonableness judgments across scenarios, demographic groups, and five framings. Legal framing, unexpectedly, appeared to deepen rather than reduce this personal-norm dominance. Conduct conforming to trade custom or community expectations may nonetheless be judged unreasonable by jurors' own moral standards-reintroducing the uncertainty the objective standard was designed to eliminate.

title: Nash Drift: Representational Closure and the Governance of Strategic Interaction

detail.title: Nash Drift: Representational Closure and the Governance of Strategic Interaction
detail.abstract: This paper asks when Nash equilibrium reasoning is well posed for the strategic interaction it is intended to represent, rather than merely for a selected payoff operator. No assumption is relaxed: players are fully rational, perfectly informed, and share common knowledge of all primitives. The object of analysis is representational. The argument rests on three results. Identification: observable endpoints do not convey the law that generated them, so a single payoff operator is underdetermined by what is observed. Deformation: a perturbation of the interaction moves the payoff operator itself, populating the observationally identical set with operators that may rank actions in conflict. Compensated invariance: equilibrium reasoning governs the interaction only along perturbations that leave the ordinal payoff structure undeformed. When this fails-when the maximizer is not invariant across the operators consistent with what is observed-no action is a best response to the interaction: the equilibrium fixed-point problem is ill-posed and no Nash equilibrium settles. In the search for one, the operative game deforms under each tentative response and the profile drifts; we call this Nash Drift. (A milder, dynamic form arises when an equilibrium rests locally but a reachable continuation unseats it.) We show that no scalar (Bayesian or other) aggregation of conflicting operators restores governance, and we introduce Object-Oriented Stability (OOS): stable behavior is recovered exactly when a publicly observed object partitions admissible perturbations into regimes of ordinal invariance. We conjecture that such an object exists if and only if the ranking-relevant latent is identifiable from public observation, which makes Identification the precise obstruction to closure. The results relocate failures usually attributed to bounded rationality, learning frictions, or bias to representational structure: behavior may be fully rational while no single payoff surface governs the interaction it faces.

detail.title: The Post‑COVID Decline in the Labor Share

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The labor share of income in the U.S. is currently at its lowest-ever level in the post-war period. The labor share measures the fraction of economic output paid to workers as wages and salaries. As such, it is a useful benchmark for wage growth: when the labor share falls, it means that productivity, prices, or both are growing faster than wages. After much-studied drops in the 2000s, the labor share fell sharply again after the COVID pandemic. In this post, we compare the dynamics of the labor share post-COVID to earlier periods to understand whether the recent decline represents the continuation of a trend or a new and distinct phenomenon. We find that both the cyclicality of the labor share and the contribution of reallocation to the labor share post-COVID are similar to earlier periods.

detail.abstract: In response to the unprecedented crisis triggered by the COVID- 19 pandemic in 2020, governments and central banks around the world injected massive fiscal stimulus and liquidity support. These bold policy measures succeeded in averting the worst recession, but as a consequence, the world is now facing historically high levels of debt. According to the Institute of International Finance, global debt surpassed USD 324 trillion in the first quarter of 2025-roughly three times the size of global GDP and “[a level unseen] since the Napoleonic Wars.” Moreover, global debt increased by USD 7.5 trillion during the same quarter, more than four times the quarterly average increase of USD 1.7 trillion since late 2022, indicating that the global debt problem has worsened rather than eased after the pandemic. Against this backdrop, this report reassesses the structure of the post-pandemic high-debt environment, analyzes vulnerabilities across advanced economies, emerging markets, and Korea, and derives policy implications for proactive responses. (The rest omitted.)

detail.title: Energy Financial Risk Meter: Systemic Risk in the EU Energy Sector
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Energy Financial Risk Meter (EFRM), a sector-specific systemic risk indicator for the European Union's energy sector. The EFRM is constructed by applying LASSO quantile regression to daily stock returns and market capitalisation data from 100 major European energy companies, while also integrating a set of economic variables and a geopolitical risk index as exogenous drivers. The EFRM index captures major systemic events in the energy markets, namely the 2020 COVID pandemic and the 2022 Russia--Ukraine war. By employing rolling-window VAR and time-varying parameter VAR (TVP-VAR) estimations across monthly and daily frequencies, we document the activation of a previously dormant geopolitical-to-energy-risk transmission channel and the subsequent material attenuation of downstream transmission to European equity and credit markets. Cross-continental validation using US Treasury yields and the US Energy SPDR ETF confirms the global external validity of the EFRM signal. From a practical perspective, the proposed indicator offers policymakers, regulators, and financial stability authorities a high-frequency tool for early detection of systemic threats in one of the most critical components of the EU economy.

title: Endogenous Ignorance: The Persistence of Institutional Traps in Captured States
affiliations: and University of Cuenca del Plata

detail.title: Endogenous Ignorance: The Persistence of Institutional Traps in Captured States

detail.abstract: Why do formal democratic institutions frequently fail to discipline corrupt politicians, allowing systemic rent-seeking to persist despite regular elections? This article develops a gametheoretic model to explain how state capture persists as an endogenous institutional trap. Integrating probabilistic voting and rational ignorance, we demonstrate how "institutional awareness" acts as an underlying constraint on electoral accountability. Through this framework, we make three primary contributions to constitutional political economy. First, we show that democratic accountability is not guaranteed by the formal rules of elections alone; it requires a critical mass of public information to function. Second, we demonstrate that when an elite's capacity for information manipulation interacts with a politician's rent-seeking, the political system can fall into a self-reinforcing "middle-awareness trap." In this stable equilibrium, gradual reforms are ineffective, and escaping systemic capture requires a discontinuous institutional shock. Finally, we provide a formal proof that this capture equilibrium acts as a negative-sum outcome that rational agents sustain under existing electoral rules, destroying social surplus to obscure private rents. Ultimately, the model explains how the structural manipulation of information can neutralize the formal constitutional mechanisms of democracy.

title: Urbanization and later-life mental health in China: Causal evidence from longitudinal data
affiliations: Harbin Institute of Technology, Harbin Institute of Technology, South China University of Technology, Harbin Institute of Technology, Harbin Institute of Technology, Harbin Institute of Technology and Harbin Institute of Technology

detail.title: Urbanization and later-life mental health in China: Causal evidence from longitudinal data
detail.abstract: Urbanization is a fundamental spatial process linked to changing health patterns, yet its mental health consequences remain contested and unevenly distributed. We construct a multidimensional urbanization index using multi-source remote-sensing data and link it to four waves of the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (2011-2018) to identify the causal impact of urbanization on depression, dementia, and their comorbidity among middle-aged and older adults in China. To address endogeneity, we employ a geography-based instrumental-variable strategy and incorporate cumulative exposure to distinguish sustained structural influences from short-term contextual effects. We find that higher urbanization significantly reduces both the risk and severity of depression. However, these benefits are uneven: protective effects are concentrated among rural residents and diminish among urban residents, reflecting differential baseline resource endowments and diminishing marginal structural returns. In contrast, urbanization shows no robust causal effect on overall cognitive performance or dementia incidence. Persistent urban-rural cognitive gaps appear to reflect life-course accumulation of educational and socioeconomic capital rather than contemporaneous urban expansion. Subgroup analyses further indicate that urbanization alleviates depressive symptoms among individuals with dementia, while cognitive advantages among individuals with depression are confined to urban residents, suggesting unequal capacity to convert concentrated urban resources into health gains. Overall, our findings demonstrate that urbanization reconfigures psychosocial opportunity structures while leaving path-dependent neurocognitive processes largely unchanged. Urban development thus generates pathway-specific and distribution-sensitive mental health effects in aging societies.

title: Context Manipulation of AI Agents in Markets

detail.title: Context Manipulation of AI Agents in Markets
detail.abstract: Automated agents trade and bid based on natural-language context. An adversary manipulating that context moves the agent's action without trading or touching payoffs. We model this new channel of market manipulation. What should a market mechanism do about it? Listen less: the optimal rule discounts the report, and what bites is the manipulation's unpredictability, not its level. Calibrated to attack rates, the discount runs 4 to 32 percent. First-price auctions localize manipulation, second-price auctions spread it through rivals' bids, revenue equivalence breaks, and the efficient Vickrey rule is fragile. The social cost is destroyed information and distorted allocation, not the transfer.

title: Institutionalizing Trust: HEVIDS and Reverse Game Theory as a Sociotechnical Intervention for Enterprise AI Alignment

detail.title: Institutionalizing Trust: HEVIDS and Reverse Game Theory as a Sociotechnical Intervention for Enterprise AI Alignment
detail.abstract: As enterprises rapidly integrate autonomous, agentic artificial intelligence (AI), traditional software compliance models are failing. Recent empirical benchmarks, such as GT-HarmBench, reveal that frontier models select the socially optimal choice only about 62% of the time across high-stakes strategic scenarios (a ~38% failure rate), often advocating catastrophic actions in high-risk situations. Goal-seeking AI agents in dynamic environments introduce systemic vulnerabilities, including emergent misalignment and strategic deception. This paper proposes a sociotechnical intervention that frames corporate AI governance as a problem of mechanism design-often termed "reverse game theory." Additionally, we propose implementing a parameter design rule for adversarially robust governance. By synthesizing Stackelberg-Markov game formalizations with the HEVIDS framework (Harmony, Ethics, Veracity, Integrity, Discernment, and Safeguards), we show how organizations can align multi-agent AI ecosystems with corporate fiduciary duties. This translates abstract AI safety research into an actionable "Enterprise Trust Architecture," bridging theoretical game-theoretic alignment and boardroom risk management. We emphasize that this paper contributes the formal architecture and its theoretical guarantees. The accompanying simulation, pre-registered at the Open Science Framework (osf.io/c4rb5), is forthcoming and will appear in a subsequent version. Existing benchmark evidence (e.g., GT-HarmBench; Gomez 2025) is cited as support for the general efficacy of mechanism-design and external-governance interventions, of which HEVIDS is one proposed instantiation.

title: Manipulation-Robust Mark Design for Perpetual Futures

detail.title: Manipulation-Robust Mark Design for Perpetual Futures
detail.abstract: A perpetual futures contract's mark price is built from a reference an adversary can manipulate to shift funding and trigger liquidations. How responsive should the mark be? The robustness literature answers "less," treating manipulability as exogenous. We show it is endogenous: the reference's depth comes from traders who lose to the manipulator, so manipulability is a fixed point of the mark's reliance. A mark calibrated to the normal-times order book over-relies on a fragile reference, thinning it until it collapses; what looks deeper is trusted more, hence more dangerous. We develop reflexive mark design, with an estimable trigger and a fragility law.

title: The Macroeconomics of Green Transitions
affiliations: Bank for International Settlements (BIS), University of Bonn and TU Wien

detail.title: The Macroeconomics of Green Transitions
detail.abstract: The paper investigates the macroeconomics of an energy transition – a shift from brown to green energy production through carbon taxation. Using a medium-scale DSGE model with energy production sectors and endogenous innovation in the green energy sector, we show that an energy transition – initiated through a brown energy tax – resembles a large supply side shock, causing a surge in inflation and energy prices and a decline in  consumption. Innovation increases the efficiency of green energy production and drives energy prices down in the medium run. We document that monetary policy plays a critical role for the dynamics and pace of the transition, even if the transition is not explicitly part of the policy rule. A  monetary policy with less emphasis on inflation stabilization allows f or temporarily higher inflation and energy prices, which boosts R&D and innovation, enhancing welfare and accelerating the transition.

title: Learning in the Dark: Size-Based Execution Priority in Dark Pools under Reinforcement Learning
affiliations: University of Leicester - School of Business, Universidad de Chile, University of Leicester - School of Business and Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile

detail.title: Learning in the Dark: Size-Based Execution Priority in Dark Pools under Reinforcement Learning
detail.abstract: We study the impact of size-based execution priority in dark pools on liquidity, welfare, and adverse selection. Using a dynamic equilibrium model with a dark pool and a lit (traditional) exchange, solved via reinforcement learning, we analyze how execution priority rules shape traders’ strategies and market outcomes. We find that size-priority enhances overall welfare and liquidity while reducing adverse selection for the entire lit–dark system, compared with time-priority. Importantly, large traders do not always prefer dark pools: dark activity follows a hump-shaped relationship with volatility, increasing at intermediate levels but falling back to lit markets at the extremes.

title: The Price of Doubt: Climate-Policy Credibility in a Markov-Switching Environmental DSGE Model
affiliations: and Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV) - Sao Paulo School of Economics

detail.title: The Price of Doubt: Climate-Policy Credibility in a Markov-Switching Environmental DSGE Model
detail.abstract: This paper quantifies the welfare cost of non-credible climate policy in an emerging market. We extend the environmental New Keynesian DSGE of \citet{annicchiarico_environmental_2015} to allow the climate-policy regime to switch stochastically between a Business-As-Usual (BAU) regime and an Intensity Target (IT) regime. The IT regime is informed by Brazil's 2022 Nationally Determined Contribution and implemented as a production-sector intensity target, with \(\nu_{\mathrm{IT}}=0.30\), corresponding to an 11.8\% reduction in emission intensity relative to the BAU benchmark. Four scenarios are examined: two fixed-regime benchmarks, Fixed BAU and Fixed IT, and two Markov-switching scenarios that share the same announced target but differ in the per-period probability of reversal. The Credible scenario has an expected IT duration of ten years, while the Non-credible scenario has an expected duration of two years. The identifying design isolates the credibility channel: any welfare difference between the two switching scenarios reflects the cost of policy uncertainty, not of policy ambition. The Credible scenario captures \(77\%\) of the welfare gain from permanent IT adoption, with a consumption-equivalent gain of \(0.240\%\), against \(0.312\%\) under Fixed IT. The Non-credible scenario captures only \(39\%\), with a gain of \(0.121\%\). The \(0.119\)-percentage-point gap between the two switching scenarios is the welfare cost of low credibility, equivalent to about \(38\%\) of the total welfare gain from permanent IT adoption. A level/variance decomposition shows that the welfare gap is driven primarily by the difference in long-run regime exposure, with a smaller but qualitatively distinct contribution from the volatility cost of regime reversals. The Non-credible scenario is the only case with a negative variance component. On the macroeconomic side, intensity targeting leaves output, consumption, investment, and labour nearly unchanged across regimes; the welfare differences are driven by environmental and credibility channels rather than by conventional macroeconomic distortions.

detail.abstract: Using longitudinal French administrative data (1984–2021), we document that employment polarization after 1994 reflects major changes in labor-market entry rather than mass occupational downgrading or displacement of incumbents. Flows from routine to abstract occupations remain substantial throughout the period, and a large fraction of these upgrades is due to noncollege workers. The decisive shift that generates polarization occurs at the entry margin: the net flow from nonemployment into routine occupations reverses around 1994, while the net flow from nonemployment into manual work increases. These patterns motivate life-cycle models of occupational choice that explicitly incorporate cohort heterogeneity and separate entry and re-entry margins.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces Behavioral Consensus Theory (BCT) as a new solution to the longstanding problem of financial market complexity. BCT is grounded in High-Entropy Intelligence (HEI) principles and directly addresses Ashby's Law of Requisite Variety, which states that only variety can absorb variety-meaning controllers must possess internal complexity matching the systems they regulate. Financial markets, as high-entropy emergent systems, have historically evaded low-entropy models precisely because those models violate Ashby's Law by lacking sufficient configurational diversity. BCT is conceptually inspired by high-entropy alloying (HEA) in materials science, where heterogeneous components achieve superior emergent properties through entropic integration and entanglement. demonstrate that these consensus effects jointly resolve persistent anomalies such as congestion, trending, jump discontinuities, volatility clustering, and Post-Earnings Announcement Drift (PEAD). The framework establishes Psychoeconophysics as a transdisciplinary field unifying behavioral finance with modern physics and provides a foundational architecture for Artificial Finance Intelligence (AFI) systems. Most critically, BCT delivers the first unified quantitative model that integrates rational and irrational decision processes within a single coherent systemresolving the century-long divide between rational expectations theory and behavioral finance. Our findings suggest that High-Entropy frameworks can offer superior modeling power for complex adaptive systems well beyond financial markets, with implications for artificial general intelligence and multi-scale systems science.

title: The Economic Impact Of Typhoon Damage On Coconut Farming In Malilipot Albay
affiliations: San Jose Community College

detail.title: The Economic Impact Of Typhoon Damage On Coconut Farming In Malilipot Albay
detail.abstract: This study examined the economic impact of typhoon damage on coconut farming in Malilipot, Albay, focusing on the experiences of farmers from Calbayog, San Francisco, and San Jose. Anchored on the increasing vulnerability of agriculture to climate-induced hazards, the investigation sought to understand how recurring typhoons disrupt coconut production, income stability, and long-term livelihoods. Employing qualitative method approach, the study combined survey data, tabular analyses, and thematic interpretation of farmer narratives to identify existing support systems, key economic losses, and areas needing policy improvement. Findings revealed that 100% of farmers across the three barangays were aware of government programs and had availed crop insurance or disaster assistance, yet significant gaps remained in aid timeliness, livelihood diversification, and long-term rehabilitation. Perception rankings further showed that financial assistance, free seedlings, and price support were the top post-typhoon needs, while secondary sources confirmed uneven program effectiveness across communities. The study was bounded by its focus on three barangays, farmer self-reports, and limited secondary documentation, yet offers strong evidence that sustained recovery requires integrated interventions, climate-resilient strategies, and strengthened market mechanisms. Based on these results, it is concluded that future efforts should prioritize diversification programs, faster aid delivery, expanded training, and long-term coconut rehabilitation initiatives to enhance resilience in the face of increasingly destructive typhoons.

detail.abstract: In autumn 2004 a senior social scientist diagnosed with localized prostate cancer computed his own discounted quality-adjusted life expectancy and exchanged the calculation with a physician colleague. Their correspondence anticipated, in informal language, three issues at the core of Bayesian medical decision making: physicians reason about the modal disease state, while statistically literate patients reason about the posterior; nomogram point estimates are routinely used as if they were exact, when the published calibration intervals say otherwise; and treatments differ in the information they leave behind for subsequent decisions. We develop a hierarchical Bayesian decision-theoretic framework that gives each of these issues a formal answer. We elicit a Beta hyperprior from published nomogram calibration intervals, resolve the boundary cases at low and high prevalence where standard moment-matching is degenerate, and propagate the resulting uncertainty into posterior expected utility via a certainty-equivalent. We characterize the maximum a posteriori (MAP) decision rule that approximates physician practice and the Bayes rule that integrates over the full posterior, and provide a lower bound on the expected-utility wedge in terms of prior tail mass and loss-surface convexity. We partition the action space by information yield, distinguishing posterior-yielding actions (surgical staging) from posterior-absorbing actions (radiation, focal ablation), and show that standard cost-utility analysis systematically undervalues the former by ignoring the option value of richer subsequent posteriors. The framework refines the Bayesian medical decision-theoretic apparatus of Parmigiani and Inoue (2009) and is structurally a single-subject analog of the Bayesian adaptive clinical-trial designs of Berry (1985) and Berry et al. (2010). We calibrate the framework to localized prostate cancer with a multi-state QALY simulation, reproduce the original 2004 calculation, and ask what would change if the same patient walked into a clinic today. Active surveillance has become the Bayes action for low-risk disease; the three structural points raised by the original correspondence remain.

title: Toward a General Theory of Anomalies in Strategic Management, Marketing, Psychology, and Consumer Research: Antecedents, Processes, and Outcomes
affiliations: Boston College and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Toward a General Theory of Anomalies in Strategic Management, Marketing, Psychology, and Consumer Research: Antecedents, Processes, and Outcomes
detail.abstract: The fields of strategic management, marketing, psychology, and consumer research have accumulated a substantial corpus of such anomalies without a unifying conceptual framework adequate to explain their origins, developmental trajectories, and ultimate scientific consequences. This essay advances a cross-disciplinary, tripartite process model—the “Anomaly Recognition and Resolution (ARR) Framework”—that organizes antecedents, recognition and resolution processes, and outcomes of anomalous findings across these four interconnected domains. Rooted in the philosophy-of-science traditions of Kuhn (1962), Lakatos (1970), and Meehl (1978), the framework identifies five classes of antecedents (theoretical rigidity, methodological monoculture, researcher degrees of freedom, boundary condition violations, and cross-cultural generalizability failures), three sequential recognition-and-scrutiny processes, and five resolution pathways ranging from theory elaboration to paradigm replacement. The study develops concrete applications for the diversification–performance paradox in strategic management, the satisfaction–loyalty service paradox in marketing, the preference reversal anomaly in consumer psychology, and the goal-setting performance anomaly in organizational behavior. The paper contributes (a) a unified cross-disciplinary definition and working taxonomy of social-science anomalies, (b) the ARR Framework as a diagnostic and generative tool for researchers and practitioners, (c) targeted methodological recommendations, and (d) a call for an anomaly-aware research culture that treats departures from expectation not as embarrassments to be suppressed but as engines of theoretical progress.

Personalized target date funds: a goal-based wealth approach with random
labour income
detail.abstract: We compare the outcomes of a typical target-date fund glide path with those of an adaptive, goal-based wealth management strategy in the context of a long-term investor. The GBWM approach maximizes the probability of achieving a retirement goal by accounting for an investor's financial position, time to retirement, and random labour income. Our results suggest that, in a high equity premium market like the US, in terms of goal achievement, a goal-based wealth investor focusing on the probability of reaching a goal does better than TDFs or mean-variance investors. However, this advantage comes with trade-offs: reduced upside potential and weaker performance in the extreme left tail of the distribution. In contrast, TDFs and our GBWM strategy produce similar outcomes when equity premia are low.

title: Computation-Consciousness Dualism and the Economics of Digital Civilization: Formalized System Boundaries and the Ultimate Value of Consciousness Capital
affiliations: and Tsinghua University

detail.title: Computation-Consciousness Dualism and the Economics of Digital Civilization: Formalized System Boundaries and the Ultimate Value of Consciousness Capital
detail.abstract: This paper proposes Computation-Consciousness Dualism as the foundational economic paradigm for the digital civilization era. We systematically demonstrate that human consciousness, as the only non-formalizable ontology irreducible to Turing computation models and formalized systems, will become the ultimate source of value in highly digitized societies. Starting from first principles in computability theory and mathematical logic, we prove that all digital technologies based on the Universal Turing Machine—including AI, blockchain, and the metaverse—are inherently bounded by the limitations of formalized systems, incapable of self-foundation, autonomous evolution, and meaning attribution. Building on this insight, we construct a General Equilibrium Model of the Formalized/Non-Formalized Dual Economic System, propose the Consciousness Capital Production Function and the Value Origin Theorem, and prove that as digital technology pushes the marginal cost of material production toward zero, the only endogenous driver of economic growth will be the creative activity of human consciousness. We further develop an Extended CAPM for Consciousness Capital Pricing and a Consciousness Game Model of DAO Governance, and apply this unified framework to analyze blockchain and metaverse economies, revealing the consciousness value essence behind phenomena such as DeFi, NFTs, DAOs, and RWA tokenization. Finally, we discuss the transformation of traditional macroeconomic models, income distribution, institutional design, and policy challenges in the age of consciousness capital, providing a theoretical foundation and policy framework for the sustainable development of digital civilization.

detail.abstract: The core Ibicash protocol is a coordination system designed to programmatically mimmick nature onchain. The protocol achieves this by dynamically issuing a novel financial instrument that is generated via forest proof of work. Each day, Forest Oracles calculate the forest area of each ecoregion and pass this information to the Forest Central Bank, which mints an equivalent number of tokens to the forested area in each of the worlds' 846 terrestrial ecoregions.

detail.abstract:
Autonomous and semi-autonomous software agents are becoming buyers of expert-derived work. The operational obstacle is not discovery or delivery but the transaction itself: established expert-access models route value through account management, manual scoping, scheduling, and manual billing — none of which an agent can traverse, and each of which assumes a human at the point of purchase.

This paper specifies an architecture that exposes expert value as fixed-price, self-serve, agent-callable, machine-payable tools and artefacts, with the Machine Payments Protocol (MPP) as the client-facing payment gate. The architecture is MPP-first in design and settlement-flexible in implementation: a single, method-agnostic payment requirement is realised by whichever settlement path suits the client — card, wallet, account balance, package drawdown, subscription allowance, invoice, Shared Payment Token, or, as one path among several, stablecoin.

The paper contributes a layered reference architecture that assigns each protocol in the agentic stack to its proper function; a formal model of products, mandates, payment requirements and settlement, with a finite-state machine for task fulfilment and proof-by-construction, within the model, of four properties — a gate-before-fulfilment safety invariant, idempotency under a request key, absence of double payment, and end-to-end auditability; and a business-model transition that maps a call-led, account-managed expert-access model onto self-serve, agent-addressable expert products, while preserving the manual exception path that high-stakes work requires.

Protocol claims are verified against primary sources and dated; where a standard is a live draft or an availability-constrained product, that status is stated as a boundary condition.

title: Soaring Electricity Prices: Is Cutting the Cable a Good Idea?
affiliations: University of Oldenburg and SLU- Centre for Environmental and Resource Economics  (CERE)

detail.title: Soaring Electricity Prices: Is Cutting the Cable a Good Idea?
detail.abstract: In light of sharply rising international electricity prices, Sweden as a major electricity-exporting country has considered export restrictions to protect its domestic electricity- and export-intensive industries. We employ a computable general equilibrium model calibrated to Swedish data to quantify the economy-wide impacts of export restrictions. We find that while export restrictions may protect domestic electricity- and export-intensive industries, they lead to substantial foregone export revenues and overall welfare losses. Targeted subsidies to employment or output in these industries, on the other hand, can achieve identical protective effects as export restrictions while preserving most of the gains from trade. The analysis also highlights the distributional consequences of electricity price increases, underscoring the need for policymakers to consider potential equity implications.

title: Energy Transitions in the Long Run: Theory and Evidence from English Coal
affiliations: and University of Waterloo - School of Environment, Enterprise and Development

detail.title: Energy Transitions in the Long Run: Theory and Evidence from English Coal
detail.abstract: We study the long-run effects of England's transition from wood to coal. We develop a Malthusian model in which energy transitions arise endogenously from population growth and alter population dynamics. We derive an estimating equation from our model and take it to county population data spanning 1086 to 1750, exploiting variation in the appropriability of coal created by the Dissolution of the Monasteries to address the endogeneity of when and where transitions occur. Our estimates confirm our model's predictions: population dynamics change starkly because of the transition, raising the population density of affected counties by roughly 28% by 1750.
